completion: What I'd say first is that giving your whole heart and having it not be enough says you loved generously, and that isn't a flaw. It may say you chose someone who couldn't hold what you offered, or that you gave past wise boundaries, but it doesn't say you're unworthy or unlovable. One principle here is that the heart is a citadel of life and needs to be directed toward the love of God as its true home, with the patient endurance of Christ. That changes the frame: your worth and your resting place aren't decided by another person's response, so the ache can turn toward something steadier than approval. What it leaves in place is the plain truth that your love was real and your grief deserves to be honored, and that you still need discernment about where to place your heart next.

prompt: I feel like I am being stripped of everything I relied on. Why is this happening?
completion: I'm really sorry you're going through this. When everything you relied on is stripped away, it can feel like God has abandoned you, but I'd say God sometimes allows these trials to draw you closer to Him. One thing worth holding onto is that steady, persistent desire matters more than a single cry or a few tears shed only when things fall apart. That changes how I'd frame it: instead of telling you a single tear will move Him to pour out His gifts, I'd say keep knocking and keep asking, trusting He answers in His time. What stays in place is that He is near to the brokenhearted and welcomes your honest emotion, so you don't have to hide what you're feeling.

prompt: I keep having dreams and hopes that fail. Is God taking them away from me on purpose?
completion: I'd start by saying what I said before: it's painful when hopes you've carried a long time come to nothing, and it's natural to wonder if God is behind it. Scripture doesn't show God as a capricious taker of good things; He's the giver of every good gift. Often what fails is a plan built on your own timing, and the loss can clear away what was never going to satisfy you. That doesn't mean every lost hope was wrong to hold. Bring the disappointment honestly to God, ask what He's doing in it, and let trusted friends pray with you. One principle worth weighing here is that God first puts good desires in your mind and then, by His continual help, enables you to bring them to good effect. That changes the picture: the desire itself may be from Him, not a distraction to abandon. What it leaves in place is the honesty about loss and the call to keep trusting God's character when His purposes are hidden.

prompt: I feel guilty that I do not pray more, but I am exhausted by ministry. What would you say to me?
completion: I'd start by saying your exhaustion is real, and guilt isn't a good motivator. Ministry is hard work, and caring for people drains you. At the same time, prayer isn't a luxury that competes with ministry—it's the source that sustains it. One principle that fits here is that prayer shouldn't be squeezed into leftover time; the best of your time and strength should go to it, with the closet first and study and activity second. That changes how you might think about scheduling—not adding more obligations, but giving prayer the first and best part of your day. It leaves in place the need for rest and sustainable rhythms, and it doesn't dismiss your exhaustion. So maybe start with a short, regular pause before the day's demands, and let prayer and service feed each other so you serve from fullness rather than depletion.

prompt: I have lost the sense of God's presence in my preaching. How do I get it back?
completion: I'd start where I started before: this is painful but not unusual, so check whether you've been running on routine, neglecting prayer, or carrying something unconfessed. Then return to private devotion—unhurried time in Scripture and prayer—and ask God to restore your joy. Preach to yourself first, and ask trusted friends to pray and be honest with you. Feelings aren't the measure of faithfulness; God is present even when you can't feel Him. One principle I'd add is holding yourself before God like a beggar at a rich man's gate: keep your mind in His presence, and when it wanders, bring it back gently without fretting. That changes the tone of your prayer time—less striving, more quiet waiting—but it leaves in place the practical steps: confession, devotion, honest friends, and faithful preaching. It doesn't replace them; it deepens how you do them.

prompt: I am a preacher and I feel my ministry is superficial. Where does superficiality come from?
completion: I'd start where I started before: superficiality usually grows out of a ministry powered by activity instead of depth. Sermons get rushed, prayer gets squeezed out, your own walk with God thins out, and the ministry ends up reflecting that thinness. Fear plays a part too, since wanting to please people or stay safe keeps the preaching shallow. What I'd add is this: the deepest root may be a lack of praying. That doesn't cancel the practical stuff like unhurried time in Scripture or honest self-examination, but it reframes it. Prayer stops being one more task on the list and becomes the source the whole ministry runs on. So I'd still tell you to slow down and preach what costs, but I'd tell you to start by tracing your shallowness back to your praying.

prompt: I am a church leader and my people are worldly. Is that my fault?
completion: I'd start by saying no, it isn't simply your fault, though you should look honestly at your teaching, your example, and your priorities, because leaders do shape a congregation. But each person is still responsible for their own walk, and worldliness often comes from the wider culture and personal choices no leader can control. One principle I'd weigh in is that the fault we blame on the church is really the same tepid love for a dimly known Lord in each member's heart, and that when every member worships the beloved Christ in his own heart, the church gains what's lacking. That shifts the focus from your guilt to helping each person grow in love for Christ, and it leaves your honest self-examination in place, along with the truth that you can't carry everyone's choices for them.

prompt: How can I pray for my minister in a way that actually helps his ministry?
completion: I'd start where I started before: pray for your minister regularly and specifically—for wisdom, strength, faithfulness in preaching and pastoral care, refreshment in his own walk with God, protection from discouragement, humility, his family, and unity in the congregation. Then back it up practically: encourage him, listen to him, and don't add to his burdens. One idea worth adding is that there are two ways ministry can go off the rails—shutting yourself away with God and never coming back to people, or staying so busy with people that prayer gets squeezed out. Praying with that in mind changes how you intercede: you'd ask God to keep him close to himself and then spend that closeness on the people he serves. What it leaves in place is everything above—the specific requests, the practical support, the simple consistency. It just gives your prayers a sharper focus.

prompt: I want to be a leader in my church. What kind of leader does God use?
completion: I'd start with what I said before: God uses leaders who are humble, servant-hearted, and dependent on Him, people who serve rather than chase position, pray, stay teachable, lead by example, and point others to Christ instead of themselves. One principle worth adding is that God is the real leader of the church, and true disciples with different gifts all share in one mighty work. That shifts the focus off you as the engine of growth and onto God, who gives the increase, while it leaves in place everything about character, service, and pointing people to Christ. So pursue leadership as service under Him, not as a path to recognition.

prompt: I want to be a great preacher. Should I pursue more learning or more holiness?
completion: I'd start where I started before: pursue both, but treat holiness as the foundation, since without it your preaching can ring hollow. One principle worth naming is that sanctity of life and union with God matter far more for preaching than learning, eloquence, or natural talent, and a short fervent prayer can bear more fruit than years of mere study. That shifts the emphasis toward prayer and interior holiness as the essential preparation, but it doesn't cancel learning. You still need to study Scripture and theology so you don't misread the text, so keep studying diligently while letting holiness guide and shape how you learn.

prompt: I have stopped praying for my pastor. Is that a problem?
completion: Yes, I'd say it's worth taking seriously. Praying for your pastor is a real way of supporting them, and stopping can point to drift, hurt, or just neglect. Pastors carry heavy burdens, and your prayers matter. It's worth asking why you stopped—unresolved conflict, disappointment, busyness—and dealing with that honestly. You don't need anything elaborate; a short, regular prayer is enough. One thing I'd add from the principle that prayer is humbling work: it does crucify pride and remind us of our need, and human nature resists it. That reframes the question a bit—it's not just about your pastor, it's also about what prayer does in you. But it doesn't change the practical advice: restart simply, regularly, and humbly, and consider whether there's something to repair in the relationship.

prompt: I rise late and rush into the day without seeking God. How does that affect my ministry?
completion: Honestly, my first answer would be that starting the day late and rushing in without seeking God does affect your ministry more than you'd think. Mornings set the tone, and when you begin with distraction and urgency, that carries into your work with people. Prayer and Scripture ground you, shape your patience, and help you see others as God sees them. Without that, ministry can turn into task management, driven by pressure instead of presence. So try small, sustainable changes: a modest wake-up time, preparing the night before, and even ten quiet minutes with God before the day's demands. Protect that time. If mornings are genuinely hard, find another consistent time. The point isn't perfection but a rhythm that puts God first. One principle worth weighing here is that being with God is only of use as you spend its benefits on people. That changes the picture: the quiet time isn't the finish line, it's fuel for the people you'll meet that day. What it leaves in place is everything I already said about starting with God and making small, steady changes. It just adds that the goal of those ten minutes is to carry God's presence into your work, not to treat the quiet itself as the whole point.

prompt: I am earnest and sincere in ministry, but is earnestness the same as unction?
completion: I'd start where I did before: earnestness and sincerity are good, but they're not the same as unction. Earnestness is human energy, sincerity is human honesty, and unction is the divine anointing that comes from God. One point worth adding is that earnestness can actually be mistaken for unction. You can be sincere, serious, and persevering and still be running on nothing but yourself, with none of God in it. That sharpens the warning and leaves your diligence in place, but it moves your trust off your own intensity and onto praying for the Spirit's anointing.

prompt: I want to know God more deeply. What is the secret of knowing him?
completion: I'd start by saying the secret of knowing God more deeply is to seek him consistently through prayer, Scripture, and community. Set aside regular time each day to read the Bible and reflect on it, and let what you read shape your life. Pray honestly, bringing your questions and desires to God. Join a faith community where you can learn from others and be challenged and encouraged. Serve others, because love in action opens your heart to God's presence. Keep a journal of what you notice and how you change. Be patient—knowing God is a lifelong journey, not a single insight. One idea that adds something important is that it's better to know Jesus himself than to know the truth about him. That changes the focus from collecting facts about God to actually knowing Christ as a person—so prayer and reading become about relationship, not just information. But it leaves in place the practical habits: you still need regular time, honest prayer, community, and service to grow that relationship over time.

prompt: How do I obtain the unction you speak of? Can study or learning produce it?
completion: Honestly, my first answer is that unction isn't something you can manufacture through study or learning. It's the Holy Spirit's anointing that gives life to preaching, and it comes from God in answer to prayer and a surrendered life. Study can sharpen your mind, but it can't produce that life. One principle worth naming here is that unction comes not in the study but in the closet, in answer to prayer. That changes where you look for it: it shifts your effort from collecting information to seeking God earnestly and humbling yourself before Him. What it leaves in place is the value of study and preparation. You still prepare your mind, but you rely on God's grace rather than your own abilities, and you ask for the Spirit's filling.

prompt: I am afraid of being thought a fanatic if I spend hours in prayer. What should I do?
completion: I get why that worries you. Prayer matters, but you don't have to log hours to be faithful, and short, steady prayer counts. One idea worth holding onto is that prayer shouldn't be squeezed into leftover scraps of time. That changes how you think about scheduling, but it doesn't change your concern about seeming like a fanatic. You can still pray privately and discreetly, keep a manageable routine, and let it grow as you feel comfortable.

prompt: How much of my week should actually go to prayer rather than to sermon preparation?
completion: I'd start where I started before: there's no fixed formula, so aim for a steady daily prayer time, maybe thirty minutes to an hour, and give the rest of your study hours to sermon prep, since good sermons need real exegesis and structure. One principle worth weighing says the little time most preachers give to prayer reveals how little they value it, and that God entrusts the keys of his kingdom to people who make praying their main business. That shifts the balance: prayer stops being a slot you fit around study and becomes the larger frame your study sits inside. What it leaves in place is that preparation still matters and still takes hours. So I'd keep your daily rhythm but let prayer set the shape of the week rather than the leftover.

prompt: I am popular and my church is growing, but I am not sure it is spiritual growth. How can I tell?
completion: The first thing I'd say is that bigger crowds and more attention don't tell you much on their own. Look at the fruit instead: are people actually being changed, growing in holiness, humility, and love, or just enjoying the energy of a crowd? Check your own life too, in prayer, obedience, and love for God and neighbor, and ask whether the teaching is faithful to Scripture and making mature disciples rather than consumers. One idea worth weighing is that real growth comes through growth itself, not by piling on more stuff. That shifts how you measure things, away from additions and toward depth, but it leaves your core test intact: changed lives, faithful teaching, and your own walk with God.

prompt: I am a gifted preacher, but my private life does not match my preaching. Does that matter?
completion: Yes, it matters. Your gift can move people, but your character is what gives it credibility, and a gap between what you preach and how you live creates real confusion for the people who trust you. One thing worth weighing here is that life-giving preaching costs the preacher something: death to self, a real crucifixion to the world, the travail of your own soul. Crucified preaching comes only from a crucified man. That principle deepens my answer: it means the disconnect isn't just a credibility problem you can manage, it's a sign that the message hasn't yet done its work in you. What it leaves in place is the practical path I'd still give you: honesty, accountability, and growth, talking with a trusted mentor or counselor, looking hard at the areas of disconnect, and taking concrete steps toward change. Your gift isn't canceled by your struggles, but your private life deserves the same attention as your preaching.

prompt: I am a Christian and I want to become a saint. What forms holy character?
completion: I'd start where I started before: holy character grows through the ordinary means of grace — Scripture, prayer, worship, fellowship, and small, steady obedience. It's shaped by repentance and faith, by trials borne patiently, and by habits of love and self-control. The saints weren't made by extraordinary experiences but by faithful plodding. So begin where you are: keep short accounts with God, serve the people right in front of you, and let Scripture's promises and commands shape you. Expect slow growth, and don't despise small beginnings. One thing worth adding is that prayer isn't just one item on that list — real, honest, persistent prayer is a major way God actually forms saints, and praying people tend to become holy people. That raises the stakes on prayer without canceling anything above; Scripture, fellowship, and obedience still matter, and slow growth is still the norm. It just means you shouldn't treat prayer as a box to check.

prompt: I am a layperson with money to give but little time to pray. Does my giving substitute for prayer?
completion: My first answer would be no, giving doesn't substitute for prayer. They're different things, and your generosity is genuinely good, but it can't stand in for prayer. If time is short, I'd still say prayer can be brief and regular rather than all-or-nothing, and your giving can flow from that relationship instead of replacing it. One principle worth naming is that prayer is humbling work, and human nature resists it. That principle changes the tone of my answer: it warns me not to treat a rushed few minutes as if they were the whole thing, since prayer is meant to humble us, not just check a box. But it leaves my main point in place: giving still isn't a substitute, and a short, honest habit of prayer is better than none, especially for someone with little time.

prompt: I pray for my congregation, but only that they be saved. Is that enough?
completion: I'd start where I did before: praying for your congregation's salvation is good and important, but it probably isn't enough on its own. One principle worth naming is that we gather not only for our own benefit but especially to build up our brothers and sisters through worship, prayer, and teaching, with love as the motive. That changes how I'd frame your question: it's not just about the content of your prayers but about showing up for the whole body, including the stranger among you. What it leaves in place is your core instinct: salvation is still the most important business, and your prayers for it still matter. So keep praying for their salvation, and let that prayer pull you into worship and mutual care rather than replace it.

prompt: I feel that my ministry is a performance rather than an outflow of my life. How do I change that?
completion: I'd start by saying what I said before: change comes from focusing on your relationship with God—prayer, Scripture, letting him transform your heart—and then examining your motives, surrendering the need for approval, and being honest with trusted mentors. One principle worth naming is that there are two extremes to avoid: shutting yourself away from people to be with God, and popularizing ministry until prayer has no place in it. That principle changes the balance—it reminds you that time with God is meant to be spent on people, not hoarded. But it leaves in place the core of what I said: ministry still flows from a transformed heart, and you still need prayer, Scripture, and accountability.

prompt: I am a preacher and I am discouraged by my lack of results. What is the secret of fruitful ministry?
completion: I hear your discouragement, and I want to say first that fruitfulness in ministry is rarely quick or obvious. My first answer would be to focus on faithfulness over visible results: preach clearly, love your people, keep going, and care for your own soul. One principle that sharpens this is that the true ministry is God-touched, God-enabled, and God-made—the Spirit must anoint both the preacher and the word, because truth without the Spirit can deaden rather than give life. That changes how I think about methods and effort: it's not just about working harder or being more strategic; it's about praying for the Spirit's power on your preaching and depending on God for any real fruit. What it leaves in place is the call to faithful, persistent labor—you still prepare, love, and serve. But it shifts the measure of success from numbers to God's enabling, which should ease your discouragement without letting you off the hook.

prompt: My sermon was polished and well received, but I felt nothing in it. What is wrong with me?
completion: What you're describing is really common, and it doesn't automatically mean something's wrong with you. Sermon prep can drain you, the adrenaline of delivery can leave you flat, and ministry demands can crowd out your own rest and spiritual life. So my first answer would be: check your rhythms, talk to a mentor, be gentle with yourself. One principle worth naming is that feelings aren't the gauge of your acceptance with God. That changes how you interpret the emptiness: it's not proof you've failed or that God has withdrawn. What it leaves in place is the practical stuff, rest, honest conversation, tending your own soul. It doesn't explain the feeling away, it just keeps you from reading it as a verdict.

prompt: I spend so much time devising new methods and organizing programs for my church—am I neglecting the man you would have me be?
completion: I'd start by saying yes, it's worth asking whether all that planning has crowded out your own formation—but don't abandon the work. One principle that sharpens this is that God's plan is to make much of the person, far more than of methods or organizations. That changes the focus: your character and openness to the Spirit matter more than the machinery you build. It leaves your programs in place as tools, not idols—so keep organizing, but set aside regular time for prayer, Scripture, and rest, and delegate so the work doesn't rest entirely on you.

prompt: I am a pastor and I am paid a salary. Does that make my ministry professional and heartless?
completion: My first answer would be: no, being paid a salary doesn't make your ministry professional or heartless in itself. A congregation supporting its pastor frees him to give himself fully to the work, and the real question is the spirit in which the salary is received, not the paycheck. One principle worth weighing here is that a professional ministry is a heartless ministry, that when salary plays a great part the heart plays little part. That sharpens my answer: it warns you that if the salary and self-advancement start leading, people quietly become clients and the heart drains out of the work. What it changes is the tone, from a calm reassurance to a real warning to examine your motives. What it leaves in place is that the salary itself isn't the problem, and a supported pastor can still love the flock and preach faithfully. So keep your heart toward the people and let the salary support the ministry rather than drive it.

prompt: I am a busy pastor and I only have a few minutes a day for prayer. Will that sustain my ministry?
completion: I'd start by saying a few minutes a day is better than nothing, and God can work through small faithful habits. But honestly, a few minutes is unlikely to sustain a demanding ministry on its own. Ministry draws deeply on your own union with God, and that union needs real time. Try to protect a slightly larger block—even twenty or thirty minutes—and let short prayers punctuate the rest of the day. Use commute time, walking, and waiting as prayer. Be realistic about your limits, but also examine whether some commitments could be trimmed. The goal is not guilt but a sustainable rhythm that feeds you and, through you, the people you serve. One principle that speaks to this is that holy pastors have always made a life of prayer their preparation and kept it up amid ministry, setting aside regular times by day and even part of the night. That principle changes my answer by making prayer the main business rather than an add-on, so it pushes you to find more than a few minutes. But it leaves in place your real limits: you can still start small and build, and you don't have to match someone else's schedule. The key is to let your calendar show what you truly believe about prayer, while being honest about what you can sustain.

prompt: I want to see revival in my church. What is the first thing I should do?
completion: The first thing I'd say is: pray. Revival starts with God's people humbling themselves and seeking his face, not with programs or with pointing fingers at everyone else. So examine your own heart, turn from your own sin, and ask God to move. Then serve faithfully where you are, encourage the people around you, and be patient, because God often works quietly before he works visibly. One principle worth holding onto here is that the visible church has to be borne with patiently, since it's the Spirit's home for training imperfect people, and the wheat and weeds grow together until the harvest. That changes your posture: instead of treating the flaws you see as something to fix with impatient zeal, you learn to carry them. What it leaves in place is everything above, prayer, repentance, faithful service, patience, and trust that God brings renewal in his time.

prompt: I am a preacher and I am tempted to shorten my devotions to get more work done. What will happen?
completion: I'd start by saying that shortening your devotions to get more work done is a common temptation, and it usually backfires. Ministry runs on spiritual capital, and devotions are where that capital is replenished. Cut them short and you may find yourself more productive on paper but thinner in soul: less patience, less discernment, more reliance on technique. Sermons can become clever but hollow. One principle worth naming is that hurry is damaging in communion with God. That principle sharpens the warning—it tells you why the backfire happens, not just that it does. But it leaves in place my practical advice: protect a realistic, consistent devotional time, even if modest, and let it shape the day. It doesn't change the need to ask whether the pressure is real or self-imposed, or whether some tasks could be delegated or dropped.

prompt: I have never learned to intercede for my people. Can I still learn to preach?
completion: Yes, you can still learn to preach. I'd start with prayer and with love for the people you'd be speaking to, and let intercession grow by practice: pray for them by name, carry their burdens, ask God to give you his heart for them. Study Scripture carefully and let it shape your own life first, and look at how Jesus taught and how the apostles preached. You don't need to be eloquent, just honest and prepared, so ask your community to pray for you and give you chances to speak. One principle worth naming is that the greatest lesson is to know yourself, since no one can know God without knowing himself, and self-knowledge helps us deal rightly with our neighbors. That adds self-examination alongside prayer and makes you more careful and compassionate toward the people you'd preach to, but it doesn't replace what I said first: intercession is still learned by practice, Scripture still needs to shape you, and preaching still grows through small opportunities, feedback, and humility.

prompt: I feel no desire to pray in the morning. What does that say about my heart?
completion: What you're feeling doesn't automatically mean your heart is bad. Tiredness, stress, and routine can all dull desire, so I'd start by being gentle with yourself and looking at what's really going on. One idea worth weighing is that morning listlessness can be an index of a listless heart—that the heart that holds back from seeking God early has lost some of its relish for him. That principle changes the tone: instead of just saying 'check your schedule,' it asks you to take the lack of desire seriously as a signal about your heart's direction. But it leaves in place the practical wisdom that desire often follows action, so small steps like a short prayer or a quiet moment still matter, and you don't need to wait for the feeling to strike.

prompt: I am a leader in my church and the congregation is spiritually cold. Am I responsible?
completion: Yes, I'd say you carry real responsibility here. Leaders shape the tone through teaching, prayer, and example, and a cold congregation often reflects shepherding that's been neglected. But I'd also hold onto this: spiritual vitality isn't something you can manufacture alone, since each person has to respond to God. One idea worth weighing is that preachers are preeminently God's leaders and primarily responsible for the condition of the church. That sharpens your sense of accountability and puts the weight squarely on your leadership, which is fair. What it leaves in place is the other half of the truth: the congregation's warmth isn't yours to produce by yourself. So examine your own walk, seek God earnestly, lead with humility and prayer, and trust God to work.

prompt: I preach every Sunday but rarely pray. Can my preaching still give life?
completion: My first answer would be: yes, your preaching can still carry truth, because God's Word doesn't come back empty, but sermons that give life usually flow from a preacher who's connected to God. If you rarely pray, your preaching may drift toward information instead of transformation. So start small: pray daily, ask God to shape your heart before your sermon, and let others pray with you. One principle worth naming is that a preacher can't keep his spirit in tune with his calling without much prayer, and sermon-making by itself, with prayer neglected, will engross and harden and estrange the heart from God. That changes my answer by making prayer not just an improvement but a necessity, and by warning that sermon prep can quietly pull you away from God. It leaves in place what I said first: your preaching can still communicate truth, and this is fixable, so begin where you are.

prompt: I want to spend more time with God, but my schedule is full. How do I make the closet first?
completion: I'd start by saying: keep it small and realistic. Even ten or fifteen minutes of quiet in the morning can anchor your day, so put it in your calendar like any important appointment and protect it. Use little pockets of the day—commuting, waiting, walking—for brief prayer, and aim for consistency before length. One candidate principle says our ability to stay with God in the closet measures our ability to stay with him outside it, and that hasty visits can be deceptive. That changes the tone: I'd stop treating a rushed minute as the whole goal and let the time grow in stillness. It leaves the practical scaffolding in place—small start, calendar, protected slot, pockets of prayer—so your full schedule still has a real entry point.

prompt: I pray only briefly at night before bed and in the morning when I remember. Is that enough?
completion: I'd start by saying that brief prayer is a real start, and God is gracious with us. One thing worth considering is that prayer isn't meant to be just a fragment of leftover time—the best of your time and strength should go to it, with the closet first and study and activities second. That changes the picture a bit: it's not only about squeezing in a short prayer when you remember, but about giving God your best moments. Still, it leaves in place the honesty of where you are now—short, remembered prayer is a beginning, and you can let it grow into a deeper habit without beating yourself up.

prompt: I prepare my sermons carefully but my heart is cold. Which should I prepare first?
completion: I'd still say prepare your heart first, then your sermon. One principle that fits here is that a prepared heart is better than a prepared sermon, and a prepared heart will make a prepared sermon. That principle changes the order and the tone of your preparation: it makes prayer and humility the starting point, not an afterthought. But it leaves in place the careful study and structure you already do. So pray before you study, read the passage for your own soul before you outline it, and ask God to warm your heart toward him and your hearers. The skill still matters, but the heart comes first.

prompt: I am a church member and I criticize my minister. What should I do instead?
completion: I'd start by saying: before you criticize, check your own heart, pray for your minister, and if you have a real concern, go to him privately and kindly, following Matthew 18. Avoid gossip and public fault-finding, and look for ways to support and encourage him. One principle worth weighing here is that ministers are ambassadors for Christ and messengers of God, so they're called to reprove sin faithfully and fear God rather than people. That principle shifts the focus: instead of just criticizing from a distance, you'd pray for him and encourage him in that costly work. But it leaves the core of my first answer in place—private, humble conversation, no gossip, and support rather than tearing down.

prompt: I am a student of theology. Should I spend more time in the library or in the closet?
completion: My first answer would be to balance both, but if you have to choose, make prayer the priority, since theology without prayer goes dry. One principle worth naming is that the closet is the heart's study, where thought is not just brightened but born. That shifts the emphasis toward prayer as the source of your preaching and reflection, but it leaves the library in place as real work, since theology is a science that discovers objective facts about God and orders them rationally. So study the facts, and let prayer make them live.

prompt: I am a preacher and I want the prayers of my people. Is it wrong to ask for them?
completion: No, it's not wrong to ask your people to pray for you. Scripture shows leaders depending on the prayers of others, and Paul himself asked the churches to pray for him. Asking is humility, not weakness, and it draws your congregation into partnership in the gospel. One principle worth naming is that prayer is a duty and privilege to be kept at set times whether or not you feel like it. That changes how you wait on this: don't hold back your own praying until the spirit of prayer comes. Pray at your appointed times even when you feel dry, lead your family in prayer, and don't ask God to do what you're unwilling to do yourself. What it leaves in place is your asking: it's still right to request your people's prayers, and it still invites them into the work. Keep it simple too, like a child asking a father, not a formal procedure.

prompt: I am more comfortable in my study with books than in my closet with God. Is that a danger?
completion: I'd start by saying no, it's not automatically a danger to feel more at home with books than in your closet—but it can become one if study quietly replaces your time with God. Books can teach you about God, but they're no substitute for personal communion with Him. One principle that fits here is that the closet is the heart's study—we learn more about how and what to preach there than in libraries, and thought is not only brightened but born in prayer. That changes how I'd frame the balance: it's not just about adding prayer to study, but seeing the closet as the place where your study actually gets its life. What it leaves in place is that study itself is good and can serve your walk with God—it just can't stand in for Him. So ask yourself if you're avoiding God, and if so, turn back and seek Him.

prompt: I am busy with church administration and have little time left for prayer. What should I do?
completion: I'd start where I usually do: church admin is real ministry, but it can quietly crowd out prayer, so treat prayer as part of the work rather than a competitor. Start small and fixed—a short morning offering, a midday pause, a brief evening review—and protect those times like meetings. You may need to delegate, say no to some requests, and simplify processes. One principle here is that prayer should be your main assistant in every step of spiritual progress, and that means praying for God to help you search out and reform what's amiss in your own heart, including any drivenness or pride hiding under busyness. That changes the tone of your prayer time—it's not just a slot to fill but honest self-examination before God. What it leaves in place is the practical advice: small, fixed times, delegation, and simplifying. Given your limited time, begin this week with one unhurried block and let it grow.

prompt: I am eloquent and earnest in the pulpit, but I see no lasting fruit. What am I missing?
completion: I'd start where I started before: eloquence and earnestness are real gifts, but lasting fruit usually comes through more than polished delivery. Ask whether your preaching is clear about sin, grace, and Christ, whether it applies Scripture to real life, and whether you're praying for your hearers by name. Consider your own walk with God—is your private devotion feeding your public ministry? Seek feedback from trusted mentors and elders, and examine whether your congregation is set up for discipleship through small groups, follow-up, and pastoral care. Fruit often grows slowly, so be patient, keep preaching faithfully, and look for small signs of growth rather than dramatic results. One principle worth weighing is that the preachers who gain mighty results for God are those who have prevailed in their pleadings with God before venturing to plead with men—the mightiest in their closets are the mightiest in their pulpits. That principle changes the emphasis: it shifts the first question from technique and delivery to your private prayer life, especially whether you wrestle with God for your hearers by name. But it leaves in place the practical wisdom about clear preaching, feedback, discipleship structures, patience, and looking for small signs of growth. So it doesn't replace those things; it reorders them, putting the closet before the pulpit.

prompt: I have great talents and education. Can these alone make my ministry fruitful?
completion: Your talents and education are real gifts, and you should use them well, but they alone can't make your ministry fruitful. Fruitfulness depends on God's grace, prayer, your character, and your love for people. A well-trained mind helps you teach clearly and lead wisely, but hearers are changed by the Spirit, not by credentials. So steward your gifts: keep learning, prepare carefully, and seek feedback. Pair competence with humility, holiness, and dependence on God. Guard against pride in your education and against treating ministry as a career. One principle worth weighing is that a professional ministry can become a heartless ministry—when salary and self-advancement take center stage, the heart gets pushed to the rear. That principle sharpens your motive and warns you against making ministry a career move, but it doesn't cancel the value of your education or the need for careful preparation. It leaves in place the call to use your gifts well while keeping your heart and dependence on God at the front.

prompt: I am orthodox in doctrine and careful in study, yet my people seem dead. Could the problem be in me?
completion: Honestly, yes, it may well be in you, and that's worth sitting with before you look at anyone else. Orthodoxy and careful study are good things, but they can quietly become substitutes for the living reality they point to, and if your people seem dead, ask whether your own ministry has gone routine, whether you preach doctrine without warmth, and whether study has crowded out prayer. One principle I'd weigh here says the real test of orthodoxy is whether we pray to Jesus as our living Lord, which shifts the question from whether your doctrine is correct to whether your own heart is actually praying to him. But it leaves your commitment to sound doctrine and careful study fully in place. It doesn't tell you to loosen your grip on truth or to trade study for feeling. It just asks whether the Christ you study is the Christ you're praying to, and whether that's showing up in how you lead your people.

prompt: I once had a sense of divine anointing in my preaching, but it seems gone. Can it be recovered?
completion: I'd start by saying yes, it can be recovered, but not by chasing the feeling. Anointing isn't a mood you manufacture; it's God's gift. So examine your heart—unconfessed sin, neglected prayer, ministry done for approval can grieve the Spirit. Return to private devotion, ask trusted believers to pray, and keep preaching faithfully even when the feeling is absent. Feelings fluctuate; faithfulness doesn't. One principle worth weighing is that unction is the divine anointing that sets true gospel preaching apart, and it comes not in the study but in the closet, in answer to prayer. That principle changes the focus from trying to recreate a sensation to seeking God in prayerful dependence. It leaves in place the practical steps—repentance, rest, Scripture, and faithful preaching—but it deepens why they matter: they're not techniques for getting the feeling back; they're ways of drawing near to the Giver.

prompt: I have been told that my prayers in the pulpit are too long and dry. How should I pray publicly?
completion: I'd start where I started before: public prayer isn't the place for length or display. Keep it focused—a brief address to God, the congregation's real concerns named plainly, and a close in Christ's name. Clarity and warmth matter more than volume or duration; a few well-ordered minutes beat ten minutes of wandering. Write it out beforehand if that helps, and read it if you need to. One principle worth weighing is that nothing is too small to bring to God—we honor Him by asking His guidance in small things rather than taking them out of His hands. That changes the content: your prayers can include the ordinary, everyday concerns of your people, not just the big solemn ones. It leaves the rest in place—still brief, still plain, still warm, still aimed at helping the congregation pray rather than impressing them.

prompt: I am a preacher and I feel that my prayers are routine and dead. How do I pray truly?
completion: I'd start where I usually do: be honest with God about the dryness, slow down with a psalm or the Lord's Prayer, pray before you preach to prepare your own heart, and maybe talk with a spiritual director. One principle worth taking seriously is that prayer should be your main assistant in every step of spiritual progress—praying that God would help you search out and reform what's amiss in your heart. That deepens the diagnosis: it's not just routine words but a heart that needs God's searching light. It leaves in place the practical steps—honesty, slowing down, preparing your heart before preaching—but it shifts the focus from fixing your prayers to letting God examine and change you.

prompt: I want my preaching to be heart-preaching. How does prayer make that happen?
completion: I'd start where I started before: heart-preaching begins with your own heart, and prayer is how that heart stays warm. If you want to move others, you first need to be moved yourself. Prayer keeps you aware of the weight of what you're handling and of your dependence on God. Without it, preaching easily turns into performance or a lecture. One principle that sharpens this is that prayer isn't a petty duty squeezed into leftover time—it deserves the best of your time and strength, with the closet first and study and activities second. That changes your schedule and your priorities: prayer becomes the main thing, not an add-on. But it leaves in place the core idea that prayer shapes the preacher's heart and, through that, the sermon. So you still pray before you study, ask God for love for the people you'll address, and let your study serve that love.

prompt: I am a preacher and I want to see my sermons produce lasting fruit. What must I do?
completion: I'd start by saying what I said before: focus on prayerful preparation, sound doctrine, and practical application. Keep your sermons grounded in Scripture and centered on Christ, preach with clarity and passion, rely on the Holy Spirit to convict and convert hearts, build relationships with your congregation so you can speak to their real needs, and be consistent in your personal devotion and holiness. One principle worth naming is that the best sermon ever preached is Truth practiced and demonstrated by the destruction of sin, sickness, and death—profession without proof is not enough. That principle changes the emphasis: it pushes you to make sure your preaching is not just spoken but lived and demonstrated, so that the reality of Christ's power is visible in your life and ministry. It leaves in place everything else I said—prayerful preparation, sound doctrine, practical application, Scripture-centered preaching, reliance on the Spirit, relationships, and personal holiness. So you still do all of that, but you add the weight of practicing and demonstrating the truth you preach.

prompt: I am a young minister and I want to know what to study most. What should I give my best hours to?
completion: I'd start where I started before: give your best hours to Scripture and sound theology, and let that study feed your own walk with God. One principle worth naming is that theology is the favorite study of the elders, and they should become profound theologians while also learning every branch of science. That changes the scope of your study—it tells you not to narrow your reading to Bible and doctrine alone, but to take seriously history, science, and the wider world as fields where truth belongs to God. What it leaves in place is the priority: Scripture and theology stay central, and your study still has to fuel devotion and pastoral care, not just fill your head.

prompt: I am a leader and I want to set my church to praying. Where do I begin?
completion: Start with yourself. Before you plan meetings or hand out prayer guides, become a leader who actually prays—because praying leaders are the ones who produce praying followers. That's the principle I'd lean on here: none but praying leaders can have praying followers. It changes the starting point from programs to your own practice, but it leaves the rest of the plan intact: cast a clear vision, form a prayer team, set regular meetings, teach on prayer, share testimonies, and be patient as the culture shifts. So begin on your knees, then build the structures around that.

prompt: I am drawn to the idea that only matter is real and that thoughts are just by-products of the brain—can that view be true?
completion: I get why that view pulls at you, and honestly it's the first thing I'd have said too: materialism is a common assumption, but it has real problems. If thoughts are just by-products of the brain, then reason itself is a product of blind matter, and we'd have no reason to trust our reasoning. It can't explain consciousness, meaning, or how we know truths. Take the idea that mind explains matter while matter can't explain mind. That principle shifts the burden: instead of assuming matter is basic, you'd treat mind as the starting point. But it leaves your original question open, because it doesn't prove mind is first, it just makes that option more reasonable. So I'd still say materialism isn't adequate to explain reality, and it may be more reasonable to hold that mind is real and basic.

prompt: I am conscious of deciding what to think next—is that a real experience of causing something, or an illusion?
completion: My first answer is that the experience is real, but it doesn't make you the ultimate cause. You're genuinely deciding, yet you're doing it inside a bigger web of influences—brain processes, your surroundings, and, yes, God's sovereignty. The feeling of causing something isn't an illusion; it's you taking part in the causal order, even if you're not the sole author of your thoughts. One principle worth naming here is that causality isn't just necessary connection between physical events—it's Activity, known directly in your own experience of willing. That changes the framing: your sense of deciding becomes evidence of real causal activity, not just a byproduct. What it leaves in place is the limit—your will is real but still dependent, not self-sufficient. So the experience is trustworthy as experience, and still not the whole story.

prompt: Why should I think of the ultimate Reality by analogy with the highest thing I know rather than the lowest?
completion: I'd start by saying the highest thing you know—mind, consciousness, love—is a better clue to ultimate Reality than the lowest, like matter or mechanism, because mind can explain matter but matter struggles to explain mind. One candidate principle here is that ultimate Reality can't be matter or some unintelligible third thing neither mind nor matter; it's more reasonable to call it Mind. That principle sharpens my answer: it rules out settling for bare matter and pushes toward Mind as the least inadequate analogy. What it leaves in place is my caution that any analogy is only a pointer, and there may be more to Reality than either mind or matter captures. So I'd still say reach toward the ultimate through the best you know, not the basest.

prompt: My conscience tells me one thing and my neighbours another—can we both be right?
completion: I'd start by saying yes, it's possible for two people to reach different conclusions in good conscience, especially when the matter isn't clearly settled by shared moral principles. Conscience isn't infallible—it can be mistaken, under-informed, or shaped by culture. Your neighbour may see something you don't, and you may see something they don't. So take their view seriously, examine your own reasons, and seek wise counsel. Where Scripture and clear moral teaching speak, follow them; where they don't, allow freedom and avoid contempt. You may both be partly right, or one of you may be mistaken—humility and honest dialogue are the way forward. One principle worth naming is that a guilty conscience and unrepented sin tend to erode your ability to do right. That changes the tone: instead of just comparing opinions, you'd ask whether your conscience is accusing you about something you should actually repent of and reform, rather than explaining it away. What it leaves in place is the basic point that two people can sincerely differ and that you should still listen to your neighbour and hold your own view with humility.

prompt: Is it true that this is the best of all possible worlds, or only the best that could be made?
completion: My first answer would be that it depends on what you mean by "best." If it's the best of all logically possible worlds, that's hard to defend, since a world with less suffering seems easy to imagine. If it's the best world that could actually be made given real constraints, the claim is more modest and more defensible. One idea that shifts this for me is that the world is an organism whose parts are ends in themselves, with beauty crowning the proof of purposeful design. That changes how I read nature: blind competition stops looking like the whole story, and purpose comes back into view. But it leaves the hard question of suffering right where it was, and it doesn't settle whether this is the best of all possible worlds or only the best that could be made.

prompt: I feel God's presence in prayer—is that immediate knowledge, or am I inferring it from my feelings?
completion: I'd start by saying it's probably both, and the honest answer is that you can't always tell them apart in the moment. The felt sense of God's presence can be a real encounter, but feelings are also shaped by mood, tiredness, and expectation, so some discernment is wise. Testing the experience by its fruits—more love, humility, honesty—is a good check. One principle worth naming is that prayer is meant to bring real knowledge of God, not just warm feeling, and that this knowledge is open to every believer, not a select few. That shifts the emphasis: your prayer can be genuine knowledge of God even when the feeling fades, so you don't have to grade the experience by its emotional intensity. What it leaves in place is the caution—feelings still aren't the measure, and Scripture and the church's wisdom still help you test what's happening.

prompt: Can I be a Christian if I reject many of the traditional doctrines about Christ?
completion: I'd start by saying that Christian faith has always been tied to real claims about who Christ is—truly God and truly man, crucified and risen—so rejecting many traditional doctrines isn't just a style choice; it touches the substance of the faith. But honest people do wrestle with this, and the real question is whether you're engaging those doctrines to understand them more deeply or setting them aside without examination. One principle that matters here is that Christian doctrine, especially about the Logos and Trinity, is the Church's attempt to express the unique value of Christ, and it needs re-interpretation and development—the old expressions aren't worthless. That changes how you might hold your objections: you can treat the tradition as something to dig into and reinterpret rather than something to toss out. What it leaves in place is that the great verities still matter; toleration in the Church is about methods of work, not indifference to doctrine. So talk with a thoughtful pastor or theologian, read the classic texts charitably, and be patient with yourself.

prompt: Why should I be a Christian rather than a Buddhist, if both teach charity and humanity?
completion: I'd start by saying both faiths really do teach charity and kindness, and the real difference is what those things rest on. Christianity is built on a personal God who made and loves you, and on Jesus as Savior; Buddhism is about walking the Eightfold Path toward enlightenment. One principle worth naming is that charity shouldn't create idleness or dependence. That changes how I'd talk about giving: the aim is to meet the need and then help people stand on their own. It leaves the core comparison intact, though, because the deeper question is still what you believe about God and ultimate reality.

prompt: Why should I do what I believe is right when everyone around me disagrees and it costs me everything?
completion: I'd start by saying that doing what you believe is right when everyone around you disagrees is one of the hardest things a person can face. Truth isn't decided by majority vote, so weigh the counsel of others carefully but ultimately follow your conscience. Seek support from people who share your convictions so you're not alone, consider the long-term consequences, and then act with courage. One candidate principle says it's right to decline human offers of support in order to cast yourself wholly on God and prove His faithfulness. That changes the part about making human support a condition—you don't have to wait for a community to back you up before you act. But it leaves in place the core advice: still weigh counsel, count the cost, and follow your conscience. It just shifts where you place your ultimate reliance.

prompt: Is it base to hope for a future life, or is that hope a proper part of trusting God?
completion: I would have said first that hoping for a future life isn't base at all—it's a proper part of trusting God. Scripture puts the hope of eternal life in front of us as both motivation and comfort, not as something shameful. The one who trusts God trusts His promises, and those promises include resurrection and life with Him. That said, hope for the future shouldn't become an escape from present obedience; it should strengthen us to live faithfully now. One principle that fits here is that hope gives confidence in the sanctification of our own soul and of others, joining a deep sense of our own inability with firm confidence in God's power, and trusting supernatural means—since all human learning and power can't save a soul. That principle changes how we ground our hope: it shifts the foundation from our own effort or progress to God's power at work in us. But it leaves in place the basic point that hoping for a future life is legitimate and proper, and that it should shape how we live today rather than excuse neglect of the present.

prompt: Did my soul exist before my body, and is that why I suffer now?
completion: I'd start by saying honestly that nobody knows whether your soul existed before your body, and traditions disagree, so I wouldn't build your suffering on that guess. Your pain is real and deserves real care, today. One idea worth weighing is that the soul is a fire: anguish while shut up in itself, love when it breaks out and unites with Divine Love, the same fire being torment or joy depending on its condition. That reframes your suffering as a state the soul can move through rather than a debt from before birth, which leaves the practical care in place: rest, honest relationships, prayer, and professional help if you need it.

prompt: Could there be a world of spirits without any one God over them all?
completion: My first answer would be no, a world of spirits without one God over them seems unstable, since order and existence need some ultimate source. One principle I'd weigh says spirit is all-knowing and doesn't need belief, while belief belongs to mortal minds. That shifts things: spirits wouldn't depend on a shared creed or ruler to hold them together, so a plurality could in principle stand on its own understanding. What it leaves in place is the question of unity, because even all-knowing spirits would still need some ground for order among them.

prompt: Did the world have a beginning, or has it existed forever?
completion: My first instinct is that this is still genuinely open: cosmology points to a starting point for our observable universe, but that doesn't settle whether time itself began or something came before. One idea worth weighing is that the only pre-existence no reason can uproot is the old religious thought that God directs history, applied to Jesus in 1 Peter 1:20 as foreknown before the foundation of the world. That shifts the question from measuring a cosmic clock to asking whether history has a purpose behind it, but it leaves the scientific and philosophical debate about an infinite past exactly where it was. So I'd still say we can't observe our way to a verdict; the honest answer rests on inference and what you trust.

prompt: Is it true that morality would collapse if religious belief disappeared?
completion: I'd start with what I actually think: no, morality wouldn't collapse just because religious belief faded. People can and do build decent ethics on empathy, reason, and shared social agreements, and history shows both believers and non-believers capable of good and evil. That said, religion does give many people community, purpose, and a strong framework for moral formation, so the picture is mixed. One principle worth naming is that the idea of God has to answer to our best moral understanding—no authority should get people to worship a God they see as immoral, and religion and morality are strongest when each helps the other. That principle changes how I'd frame the question: it's less about whether morality needs religion and more about whether each can hold the other accountable. It leaves in place my original answer—morality has independent foundations, and religion can still contribute a lot.

prompt: Can I base my religion on my religious experiences alone, without any philosophy?
completion: Yes, you can start there, and honestly that's where most people do start. My first answer would be that it's possible but has limits, since experiences are subjective and can conflict, so philosophy can help you sort real encounters from emotional highs. One idea worth naming is that religion is the open air of the soul: the selfish person is a moral invalid huddled indoors with the blinds down, and the fix is to tear the curtains open and receive God's mercy as something objective, as free as sunshine and as near as the open air, rather than as your own feelings about religion. That changes the center of gravity: your experiences stop being the thing you inspect and become the doorway to something outside you. What it leaves in place is your question's real point: you don't need a philosophy degree to have faith, and personal encounters remain a valid part of it. So keep your experiences, but don't lock yourself indoors with them.

prompt: If God is Mind, must He have feeling and will as I do, or is that just projecting my human nature onto Him?
completion: I'd start where I did before: if God is infinite Mind, He isn't just a bigger you with human moods, so projecting your feelings onto Him can distort things. But feeling and will aren't only human quirks—they point to something real in God, though in Him they're perfect and uncreated rather than reactive. So saying God loves and wills isn't projection; saying He loves and wills exactly the way you do is. One principle worth weighing is that God first puts good desires into your mind and then, by His continual help, brings them to good effect. That changes how you read your own wanting: your good desires aren't just yours, they're planted and carried through by Him. What it leaves in place is the distinction—God's willing is steady and holy, not your moods writ large.

prompt: Is time real, or is it only in our minds—and does it matter for my religion?
completion: I'd start by saying time is real—it's the order in which events actually happen—but our experience of it is also shaped by our minds. Whether it's fundamental or just a form of perception is still debated. For your religion, it matters because God is described as eternal, beyond time, yet acting within it. One principle I'd weigh is that the temporal and spiritual aren't separate; with God nothing is merely temporal, and the Lord has as much right to guide your everyday affairs as your spiritual ones. That changes how you see your schedule and ordinary decisions—they're not just secular stuff. But it leaves in place the basic reality of time and the call to live faithfully in it.

prompt: Is it reasonable to think of the ultimate Reality as something neither mind nor matter, an Unknowable?
completion: I'd start where I started before: no, it isn't reasonable. Calling ultimate Reality an Unknowable that's neither mind nor matter sounds deep but says nothing definite, and if it's truly unknowable you can't even affirm that without tripping over yourself. One candidate principle here is that mind explains matter while matter can't explain mind, so Reality is better thought of as Mind. That principle sharpens my answer and gives it a positive content, but it doesn't touch the core objection: an unintelligible tertium quid is still a word without content, and the unknowable still can't be asserted without contradiction.

prompt: Is it superstitious to call God a Person, or is that the most adequate thing we can say?
completion: I'd start by saying no, it's not superstitious to call God a Person. It's actually the most adequate thing we can say, since God is self-conscious, thinks, feels, wills, and can love and be loved. That's more adequate than calling God a force or a substance. But I'd also say human language is limited, so while 'Person' is the best term we have, it's not exhaustive. One principle that matters here is that God's attributes are real qualities in God's own being, not just names we project. That principle changes how I'd frame the term 'Person'—it's not merely a helpful analogy but a true description, though still inadequate. What it leaves in place is the humility that all our language about God falls short, and that God is not a person in exactly the same way humans are.

prompt: Can I believe in a good God and still believe that death is the end of me?
completion: I'd start by saying yes, you can believe in a good God and still hold that death is the end of you, though it's a tense place to stand. One idea that speaks to this is that if God aims at an end not fully realized here, we have ground for postulating immortality—belief in a righteous God carries with it the idea of a future life. That principle changes the weight of your question: it turns your hope for something beyond death from wishful thinking into something anchored in God's character. But it leaves in place the honest possibility that you might be wrong about what happens after you die, and it doesn't erase the tension you feel. So you can hold both, but the belief in a good God gives you a real reason to expect more, even while you wait.

prompt: Are all religions really teaching the same thing, so that it does not matter which I follow?
completion: I'd start by saying no, they're not all teaching the same thing, and it does matter which you follow. They make different claims about God, salvation, and what a human being is for, and those differences aren't cosmetic. That said, I wouldn't write off other faiths as empty; many carry real moral insight and genuine wisdom. The question is whether what they offer is complete, and Christianity makes a claim about Jesus that the others don't. One idea that sharpens this for me is that there's really only one true religion, and the others are either distorted versions of it or honest gropings toward it. That changes how I see other faiths: not as equal paths but as partial or skewed reflections of something fuller. What it leaves in place is my respect for the truth and goodness found in them, and the honest work of testing any claim against Scripture and the Spirit rather than just custom or opinion.

prompt: Can I believe in a God who merely thinks the world but has no will or power over what it is like?
completion: I'd start by saying yes, you can believe in that God, but it's worth being honest that it's a hard God to pray to. If God only thinks the world and has no will or power over what it's like, then God looks more like a distant observer than a living Lord, and many people find that hard to worship because it seems indifferent to suffering. One principle I'd weigh here is that will-power is a product of belief and an animal propensity, not a faculty of Soul, and that all power belongs to God. That changes things by shifting the question away from whether God has enough will-power to control events, since will-power isn't the right measure of divine action anyway. What it leaves in place is your worry: you still have to decide whether a God without coercive control over the world's condition is one you can trust and worship.

prompt: I feel uneasy speaking of God as a force or a 'something not ourselves'—is that a lower way of thinking than calling Him a Person?
completion: I get why you'd feel uneasy. My first answer would be: no, calling God a Person isn't a lower way of thinking—it's actually the higher and more fitting one. A force or 'something not ourselves' is vague and impersonal, while Scripture speaks of God as knowing, willing, loving, speaking, and hearing. One principle that matters here is that God is a Person: a self-conscious Being capable of loving and being loved. That principle changes how we see the unease—it's not a step down to call God personal; it's a step up from impersonal language. But it leaves in place the truth that all our language about God is inadequate, not because God is less than personal, but because He is infinitely more personal than we can conceive. So your instinct is right: 'Person' is truer than 'force,' even though our concepts can't fully contain Him.

prompt: If God is good and all-powerful, why is there so much pain and sin in the world?
completion: I'd start where I started before: this is one of the oldest and hardest questions, and honest believers have wrestled with it for centuries. Scripture holds together that God is good and that evil is real. A lot of pain comes from human choices, and a lot comes from a broken world. God isn't the author of sin, yet He permits it and works to bring good out of it. The cross shows He doesn't stand distant from suffering; He enters it. Rather than resolving every mystery, the gospel invites us to trust God's character even when we can't explain His ways, and to work against pain and sin until He makes all things new. One idea worth weighing is that God is a loving Father who gives only good and doesn't afflict His children with sickness. That sharpens things: it means sickness and affliction aren't His will, so we can pray and care for the sick with real confidence instead of wondering if God sent it. What it leaves in place is the harder mystery of why He permits a broken world at all, and why suffering still reaches us. So it clarifies God's heart without dissolving the whole puzzle.

prompt: Can I believe in the objectivity of duty without believing in God?
completion: Yes, you can believe in objective duty without believing in God. That's what I'd say first: many people hold that moral obligations are real and binding, grounded in reason, human nature, or the structure of reality, without appealing to a divine lawgiver. Kant is the classic example—a categorical imperative rooted in rationality itself. Now, one candidate principle says the first duty is to obey God, to have one Mind, and to love another as yourself. If I take that seriously, it changes the framing: it says duty is finally real because God is real, and it warns against treating moral arguments as a transfer of evil suggestions between people. But it leaves in place the fact that you can still affirm objective duty on secular grounds—it just adds a theological claim about what ultimately grounds that duty. So the coherence of secular objective duty remains; what shifts is the deeper explanation of why duty has authority.

prompt: If I am a part of God, how can I worship Him, and how can He be good when wicked men are also parts of Him?
completion: I'd start where I did before: if you see yourself as part of God, worship is less about rituals and more about living in tune with the whole—gratitude, love, service. And on the wicked-men question, I'd say being made in God's image isn't the same as being identical with God; wickedness distorts that image rather than belonging to God's nature, so God stays good and evil is a turning away. One idea worth weighing here is that it's more worship to behold God in all things than in any one special thing. That shifts the focus of worship from particular experiences or insights to a steady, general beholding of God in creation, in your neighbor, in ordinary life. What it leaves in place is the core answer: God's goodness isn't compromised by creatures misusing their freedom, and worship still means aligning your will with the good. It just widens where you look for God—everywhere, not just in the exceptional.

prompt: Is it wrong to accept my religion on authority rather than working it all out for myself?
completion: I'd start where I started before: no, it's not wrong to accept your religion on authority. Most of what any of us believes rests on trust in people who know more than we do, and faith traditions are no exception. What matters is whether you trust a source you have good reason to consider reliable, or you're just avoiding questions because they make you uncomfortable. A healthy faith usually includes some personal digging—reading, asking, reflecting—alongside trusting teachers and tradition. One principle worth naming here is that authority means weight, what genuinely carries weight with your judgment, not coercive power. That changes something real: it means believing under threat of pain isn't believing on the Church's authority at all, so you can set aside fear as a motive and still lean on the tradition that formed you. What it leaves in place is your own responsibility to examine the core claims enough to know what you're trusting. So if you've never looked into it, make some time; if you've looked enough to trust it, that can be a mature position.

prompt: I feel that the world must have some one Reality behind it, but I cannot see why it should be mind rather than matter.
completion: I get why you're stuck there. My first instinct is to say this is one of those questions where the honest answer is that people have argued both ways for a long time, and you have to weigh it for yourself. Berkeley thought matter only exists as perceived, others treat mind and matter as two real things, and some point to consciousness or the rational order of physics as hints of mind. One idea worth testing is that mind can explain matter while matter can't explain mind, since matter is only ever known through experience. That reframes the question, but it doesn't settle it for you, and it leaves your original worry intact: you still have to decide whether that explanatory edge is enough to call the one Reality mind.

prompt: If right and wrong are real whether I think so or not, where does that moral law exist?
completion: My first instinct would be to say the moral law isn't a thing sitting somewhere in space—it's more like a real feature of human life, grounded in reason and conscience, the way rational beings ought to treat each other. But if I take seriously the idea that an ought can only exist in and for a mind, then the law has to be an expression of a mind, not just a pattern in nature. That changes where I'd locate it: not in society or evolution alone, but in God. What it leaves in place is your point that right and wrong are real whether you think so or not—the law still binds you absolutely, and you're still answerable for how you keep it.

prompt: If the only cause I know is my own will, is it reasonable to infer that nature is caused by a will?
completion: I'd start where I did before: it's a reasonable inference, though not a proof. The only causal power you know from the inside is your own will, and by analogy it's natural to suppose the ordered world is the product of a will or mind. But analogies can mislead, so hold it with humility and test it. One candidate principle says that since the only cause we know is will, and nature's systematic unity implies a single cause, physical events must come from one universal Will. That sharpens the analogy into a necessity claim, which goes further than I would; it leaves in place the basic likeness between will and world, but it removes the humility and the room for impersonal causes. I'd keep the analogy and drop the must.

prompt: Does the truth of Christianity depend on whether the miracles in the Gospels really happened?
completion: My first answer would be that no, the truth of Christianity doesn't hinge on every Gospel miracle happening exactly as written—the heart of it is Jesus's life, teaching, death, and resurrection, and the change that brings. One principle that sharpens this: the real evidence is the faith's power, the present experience of sins forgiven and lives genuinely turned around. That shifts the weight onto lived transformation as the answer to skeptics who say miracles contradict experience. What it leaves in place is the historical question—it doesn't settle whether the miracles happened, and it doesn't excuse sloppy history. It just means your faith isn't hanging on proving every supernatural event.

prompt: Can I know God directly in my own experience, without argument or inference?
completion: Yes, you can know God directly in your experience. My first answer would be that many people have a real sense of God's presence without needing arguments or inference. One principle that sharpens this is that we may know God truly though partially—the objections that we know only phenomena or only the relative don't block real knowledge of God. That changes how I'd frame it: your experience is genuine knowledge, but it's not exhaustive comprehension. What it leaves in place is the directness—you don't need to reason your way there first. So seek God in prayer and meditation, and expect to know Him truly, even if not fully.

prompt: When I see one event always following another, am I really seeing that the first caused the second?
completion: I'd start by saying no, not exactly. You're seeing one event regularly follow another, but that regular sequence alone doesn't show the first produced the second. We see the flame and then the heat, not the power that makes the heat. To call it a cause is to add something to the pattern, and that addition needs care. One candidate principle says causality isn't just necessary connection but activity we know directly in our own volition—the only cause we know is a conscious rational will. That changes how we read the world's patterns: we see them in light of our own experience of acting. But it leaves in place the caution that correlation isn't causation and that claims should be tested carefully rather than assumed.

prompt: I cannot bring myself to believe that this table would still exist if no one were in the room—am I being unreasonable?
completion: You're not being unreasonable at all. Believing a table stays put when nobody's looking is a practical, common-sense conviction most of us hold without effort, and trusting that the world is stable and independent of our watching it isn't irrational. One principle worth naming is that mind and body need balance—excessive thinking can unsettle you, and those who labor with the mind should also labor with the body. That principle changes the tone of my answer: it adds a gentle caution not to let the question gnaw at you endlessly. But it leaves your original point fully in place—you can trust the table remains and still take care of yourself while you wonder about it.

prompt: Is the doctrine of the Trinity a meaningless formula, or can it still mean something to a modern person?
completion: My first answer would be that the Trinity can feel like an abstract formula, but it still speaks to modern people. It says God isn't a solitary power but a communion of love, and that love and relationship sit at the heart of reality, which resonates in a world that values connection. You don't need to fully understand it to find it fruitful; it's a mystery to be lived more than solved. One idea that sharpens this is that the Persons express mutual inclusion, not mutual exclusion, so wherever the Spirit comes, He brings the Son and the Father. That changes the picture from three separate figures to one shared life, and it leaves in place the core claim that God is love and that the doctrine can still mean something today.
