prompt: If colours and sounds only exist for minds, what becomes of the solid, shaped objects I touch and handle?
completion: I'd start by saying that colours and sounds may depend on the mind, but the objects you touch and handle aren't dissolved by that. When you touch something solid and shaped, you're in contact with something real that resists you and behaves in regular ways. One candidate principle here is that matter can't exist apart from mind, since all we know of matter—sensations and relations, including space—implies mind. That principle changes how I'd frame the object's reality: it's not independent of mind, and spatial relations themselves imply a mind that knows them. But it leaves in place the solid, shaped thing you handle as real and regular, not an illusion.

prompt: If Jesus never claimed to be God, what am I to make of the Creeds that say He is?
completion: I'd start by saying the Creeds are the church's way of putting into careful words what the New Testament says in various ways—Jesus as Lord, Savior, and Son of God—so they're drawing out what the texts imply rather than inventing a new figure. One idea worth weighing is that Jesus bears the same name as God, ho kurios, so you'd think of him as you think of God—yet he was never placed on an equality with the Father, because monotheism guarded against that. That changes how you read the Creeds: they're guarding a distinction, not flattening it. What it leaves in place is the church's settled summary of who Jesus is, which you can hold alongside Scripture.

prompt: If my conscience has grown and changed through history, can it still be a revelation of God's mind?
completion: I'd start by saying yes, a conscience that grows and changes can still reveal God's mind. A child's sense of right and wrong matures without the underlying truth shifting, and our moral awareness can deepen the same way. One principle that matters here is that the Spirit's witness in your heart bears record of the living Redeemer and exceeds other evidence, so you're not stuck depending only on the past. That changes where you look for certainty: not just at history or at your own moral progress, but at Christ risen, known directly. It leaves the growth of conscience in place as real learning, not as proof that conscience is just a human invention. Test it against Scripture and the church's teaching, and don't wait to feel more before you act.

prompt: If I have a strong feeling that something is true, does that make it a revelation from God?
completion: My first answer would be: no, a strong feeling doesn't automatically make something a revelation from God. Feelings come from lots of places, including emotions, experiences, and our own desires, so they need testing. One principle worth naming is that no one can know the things of God except by the Spirit of revelation, and every faithful person may receive that witness for themselves. That principle changes the picture by saying the real test isn't how intense your feeling is but whether the Spirit is actually giving you light, and it leaves in place the caution that raw emotion alone proves nothing. So pray for that witness, check it against Scripture, and talk it through with wise believers.

prompt: If God is limited in power, how can I be sure the world will turn out good on the whole?
completion: I'd start by saying that if God's power is limited, your worry makes sense—the future really is open, and that can be scary. But I'd still point to God's character: He's good and faithful, and He'll do everything He can to bring about a good end, even if He doesn't control everything. One principle that matters here is that God won't let us settle for less than His highest will—we're called to keep the standard high and not water it down to match our failures. That principle sharpens our responsibility: it means we can't just passively wait for God to fix things; we have to cooperate with Him and aim for His best. But it doesn't change the core hope—God's love won't fail, and He's still working within the limits of nature and human freedom. So the future is open, but God's goodness is constant, and that's where your confidence can rest.

prompt: What does it even mean to call God omnipotent—could He make two and two equal five?
completion: I'd start by saying omnipotence means God has all power, but that doesn't mean He can do nonsense. 'Two and two equal five' is a contradiction, not a feat of power—power is the ability to do something real, and a contradiction isn't a thing at all. So no, He can't make it so, not because He's weak but because the statement describes nothing. One candidate principle here is that omnipotence is power to do all things that are objects of power, and it excludes self-contradiction and things contrary to God's nature. That principle sharpens the answer: it adds that God isn't compelled to exercise all His power and can freely limit Himself, so omnipotence isn't a restless need to do everything. What it leaves in place is the core point—the impossible stays impossible, and God's inability to do nonsense is no limit on His power.

prompt: If everything I know is always matter plus my own mind, how can I be sure there is any matter at all?
completion: I'd start with the honest answer: you can't prove matter exists independently of your mind, but you have good reason to trust it, because your experience is stable, shared with others, and predictable in ways you don't control. Now take one candidate principle, that matter can't exist apart from mind, since everything you know of matter, including space and relations, implies a mind that knows it. That changes the framing: instead of asking whether matter exists on its own, you'd ask whether the mind-dependent picture still accounts for the order and sharedness you notice. What it leaves in place is that order and sharedness, which still need explaining. So the practical answer stands: certainty about an external world may not be required, and well-justified belief is enough for daily life.

prompt: Am I really a fellow-worker with God in a real struggle against evil, or is the struggle a sham?
completion: I'd start by saying the struggle is real if it actually costs you something—if it changes your choices, your habits, and your relationships, not just your feelings. One idea worth weighing is that the practical answer to evil isn't an intellectual explanation but proportion: stepping back from fixating on sin to the greater reality of God's goodness, so that studying evil doesn't intoxicate or paralyze your will. That changes how you fight—you fight from confidence in God's goodness rather than from obsession with the darkness—but it leaves your original test in place: the struggle still has to show up in real change, real resistance, real repair. So keep testing your life against what you profess, and let the evidence of genuine change encourage you.

prompt: Are my moral judgements just my feelings, or can they be objectively true like arithmetic?
completion: My first answer would be that your moral judgements aren't just feelings. Emotions show up, sure, but moral truths can be objective the way arithmetic truths are independent of what you happen to prefer. They're not identical to arithmetic, though, because they involve values and persons. Many philosophers hold that there are real moral facts, and from a Christian view those facts are grounded in God's nature, so your judgements can be objectively true when they line up with his moral order. One principle I'd weigh here says the ground of moral obligation is God's holiness, not power, not utility, and not the nature of things. That changes the foundation: right is right because God is it, not merely because he wills it or because it's useful. What it leaves in place is your original question's core: yes, moral judgements can be objectively true, and your feelings may come along for the ride without being the whole story.

prompt: Is it impious to say that God could not make a world without evil in it?
completion: I'd start by saying it's not impious to ask, but the answer matters: saying God couldn't make a world without evil does seem to limit his power, though a lot turns on what we mean by evil and freedom. One principle worth weighing is that evil is the unlikeness of God, so if good is real, evil is unreal and only seems real when we give reality to what isn't. That changes the question from a contest of powers to a matter of what's real, but it leaves in place the honest worry about whether calling evil unreal dismisses real suffering.

prompt: Is my mind a part of God's mind, so that when I think it is God thinking in me?
completion: I'd start by saying your mind isn't simply a piece of God's mind. Scripture puts God's thoughts far above ours, and when you think, it's you thinking, even though God may guide and illuminate your mind by His Spirit. One idea worth weighing is that under this dispensation we shouldn't use the lot to figure out the Lord's mind; we seek it through prayer and the Scriptures, since the Spirit now teaches believers. That changes the practical advice: instead of suggesting lots when a decision is unclear, I'd point you to prayer, the Word, and the Spirit's teaching. What it leaves in place is the core answer: God influences and directs your thinking, but your mind isn't a fragment of His.

prompt: If Christianity keeps developing, how can I be sure it will not one day be outgrown?
completion: I'd start where I did before: yes, Christianity has developed a lot over the centuries, and that's a sign of something alive, not something on its way out. The core has held steady—Christ, grace, Scripture—even as the forms kept changing, so your confidence can rest on him rather than on customs staying frozen. One principle worth naming is that doubt is a nearly inevitable stage for thoughtful believers and deserves sympathy plus a clear, orderly look at the history, not a brush-off. That changes the tone: your question gets treated as a doorway to maturity rather than a threat. What it leaves in place is the substance of my first answer—development still means growth, not obsolescence, and the center still holds.

prompt: How can I know anything about God's character from looking at nature, which seems so cruel and full of suffering?
completion: I'd start by saying nature can tell you something about God, but it's a limited and ambiguous teacher. Its beauty and order point to a Creator, yet its cruelty and suffering raise real questions. The Bible acknowledges that tension and points beyond nature to Christ, who reveals God's character most fully. So nature can stir wonder and gratitude, but it shouldn't be your primary source for knowing God. Look to Scripture and to Jesus, who shows us a God who suffers with us and promises to make all things new. Nature's cruelty is a sign of a broken world, not a revelation of God's heart. One idea worth weighing is that the more honestly you know your own misery, the more fully you can behold God's majesty. That changes the frame: the problem of suffering isn't only out there in nature, it's also in you, and humility sharpens your sight. But it leaves the core answer in place. Nature still isn't a reliable portrait of God's heart, and Christ still is. Self-contempt doesn't explain why animals suffer; it just keeps you honest while you look.

prompt: How can a new planet have existed before any astronomer saw it, if nothing exists apart from mind?
completion: I'd start by saying that if nothing exists apart from mind, the planet isn't sitting there independently of consciousness—but that doesn't mean it only pops into being when an astronomer looks. Mind here isn't just one person's private thoughts; it's the universal intelligence everything subsists in, so a planet can be there in that Mind before any human spots it, the way a truth is true before anyone states it. Discovery is recognition, not creation. One candidate idea is that God the Lord directs history, as with Christ foreknown before the foundation of the world and manifested for our sake. That principle gives the pre-existence a real grounding—it's held in divine foreknowledge and purpose, not dependent on any observer. What it changes is the reason the planet can precede discovery: it's ordered and known within that directing Mind. What it leaves in place is your starting point—nothing exists apart from mind—and the point that the astronomer's seeing is recognition, not bringing-forth.

prompt: How can I tell whether a new religious idea that came to me suddenly is from God or not?
completion: I'd start by saying: test the idea against Scripture and the teachings of your faith community, look at its fruits—does it lead to love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness, and self-control?—pray for discernment, seek wise counsel, and be patient rather than acting hastily. One principle worth naming is that belief in God isn't the conclusion of a demonstration; religion existed before argument, and proofs confirm faith rather than create it. That changes how much weight you give to trying to prove or disprove the idea intellectually—it shifts the emphasis toward the kind of life the idea produces and the habit of turning toward God. What it leaves in place is the practical testing: Scripture, community, fruits, counsel, and patience still matter. So I'd still say don't rush, and if the idea persists and bears good fruit over time, it may well be from God.

prompt: I am a wife and my husband is unconverted; what should my prayers for him be?
completion: I'd start by saying pray for your husband's heart to be opened, for God to draw him to faith, and for wisdom to love him well with patience and grace—without nagging. Pray for softness where there's resistance and for people who can speak truth into his life. Also pray for yourself, that you wouldn't grow bitter or anxious, and trust God's timing. One principle here is that prayer should be our main assistant in every step of spiritual progress, so pray that God would help you search out and reform whatever is amiss in your own heart. That principle deepens your prayers by turning some of the focus inward, but it leaves in place the core prayers for your husband's conversion and for your own patience and kindness.

prompt: I want to be saved but I am afraid of what my family will say—must I obey them or God?
completion: I'd first say that you should follow your conscience and obey God rather than your family, even though honoring them matters. One principle that shapes this is being slow to take new steps and seeking to have no will of your own, ascertaining God's will through prayer and the Word. That principle changes how you move forward—it adds patience, prayer, and testing rather than rushing—but it leaves in place the core call to obey God over family when they conflict. So pray, search the Scriptures, and then act with trust in God's help.

prompt: I have prayed for my husband for years and nothing has changed—why does God not answer?
completion: I first want to say: it can be deeply discouraging to pray for years and see no change. My first instinct would be to say that God's timing isn't ours, that He may be working in ways you can't see, and that you should keep praying while also examining your own heart. One principle that stands out to me is that God sometimes denies a petition in kindness, and we must resign our will to His, trusting that He gives what is infinitely better. That principle changes the tone of my answer: instead of just saying 'keep praying and trust His timing,' it invites you to consider that a 'no' or 'not yet' might actually be a loving answer, not a failure. But it leaves in place the core encouragement to keep praying and to trust God's goodness, even when the answer isn't what you hoped for.

prompt: I have money that I feel God wants me to give up, but I am not sure—must I obey before I get the blessing?
completion: I'd start where I did before: don't rush this. God isn't a vending machine, and blessing isn't a payout for obedience—Scripture ties the two together as relationship, not transaction. So test the impulse prayerfully: is it God, guilt, or fear? Get wise counsel, give cheerfully and freely, and don't feel you must act before your heart has peace. One principle worth weighing here is that money for God's work should be gathered in God's way—no arm-twisting of believers, no appeals to unbelievers, no slick schemes—and gifts refused if the motive is impure or the money isn't really the giver's to give. That sharpens how you'd give, not whether you must give before you're sure. It leaves your freedom intact: no compulsion, no deadline, and no blessing held hostage to a rushed decision. Pray, wait, and act when you're settled.

prompt: I have an evil habit that overcomes me again and again—must I be free of it before I can believe?
completion: No, you don't have to be free of the habit before you believe. Faith in Christ is the starting point, not the reward for good behavior. God accepts you as you are and will help you overcome the habit through His Spirit. One thing worth adding: when you've gone a while without thinking of God and then slip, don't let that spiral into disquiet—acknowledge your wretchedness and return to Him with greater trust. That changes the tone of the answer, from "get clean first" to "come back quickly," but it leaves the core in place: your acceptance isn't based on your performance, and freedom may still come gradually.

prompt: I have come near to this blessing many times and drawn back; can I still enter in?
completion: Yes, you can still enter in. Drawing back many times doesn't disqualify you; it actually shows you've seen the blessing and wanted it, even when fear held you back. God's invitation isn't withdrawn because you hesitated. The real question now is what keeps pulling you back—fear, unbelief, or something you're unwilling to let go of. Bring that honestly before God and, if it helps, before a trusted believer who can walk with you. The door is still open, and the One who calls you is patient. Take one concrete step toward Him today instead of waiting for perfect courage. One thing worth weighing: we tend to hold onto things that others could use but we don't really need, and keeping them can cost us blessing. That's worth looking at honestly—it might change how you see what's blocking you, though it doesn't change the fact that the door is open and God is patient with you.

prompt: I have a besetting sin of impure thoughts—can God cleanse even my thoughts?
completion: Yes, God can cleanse your thoughts—his cleansing isn't limited to outward actions; it reaches the mind where sin starts. Impure thoughts are often habitual, and habits of thought can be retrained. Start by noticing when the thoughts come up without beating yourself up, then deliberately turn your attention to something worthwhile. Prayer, Scripture, and honest accountability help. Practical steps—limiting what feeds your imagination, avoiding triggering situations, filling idle time—can make a real difference. Progress is usually gradual, and setbacks don't mean failure. God is patient, and the fact that you want to be cleansed is itself a sign of grace at work. One idea worth weighing is that the soul resting in God desires only him, and if some of this turmoil is delusion, it belongs to God to remedy it. That changes the pressure you put on yourself: the struggle stops being a self-managed project, and you can leave the outcome to God. What it leaves in place is the practical work—noticing the thought, refusing it, and turning toward what's pure. So keep bringing the thoughts into the light and asking for help; over time your mind can be renewed.

prompt: I have a thorn in the flesh and a temper I cannot master—is this sin that keeps me from holiness?
completion: I'd start by saying that having a thorn in the flesh and a temper doesn't automatically mean you're living in sin. Paul had his thorn, and God's grace was enough for him. Temper becomes sin when you give in to it, but it's also a weakness you can work on. Holiness is a process, and God is patient. One principle that matters here is that sin offers no real pleasure—it's a deception. That truth can strengthen your moral courage to master your temper, because you stop buying the lie that losing it will bring relief. What it changes is your motivation: you fight the temper not just by willpower but by seeing through the false promise. What it leaves in place is the need for prayer, self-discipline, and accountability, and the assurance that God's strength is made perfect in weakness. So don't be discouraged—keep pressing on, and if your temper harms others, confess and repent.

prompt: I am too shy and stiff to talk naturally about religion—how can I become natural?
completion: Feeling shy about talking about religion is really common, and the fix isn't to force yourself to become a different person. Start small: practice with trusted friends in low-pressure settings, prepare a few simple, honest sentences about what your faith means to you, and lean on listening and asking questions to take the pressure off. One idea worth holding onto is that we come into personal contact with Jesus the same way we make any friend—by thinking about Him, spending time with Him, and forming brief mental pictures of walking beside Him. That changes how you prepare: instead of rehearsing arguments, you'd build a quiet habit of companionship, which makes your words come out more naturally. It leaves in place the practical stuff—low-stakes practice, honesty, listening—so you're not adding a new burden, just a warmer center to what you're already doing.

prompt: I am weak in body and mind; does God require me to be perfect in these things?
completion: What I'd have said first is that God doesn't require you to be perfect in body or mind to earn His love. He knows we're dust, and He asks for faithfulness, not flawlessness. One principle worth naming is that perfection isn't reached just by piling up prayers and good works—self-love can feed on those unless we watch our hearts and root out habitual imperfections. That principle changes the focus: it's not about doing more, but about letting God work on the hidden attachments and habits that keep us from Him. What it leaves in place is the core answer: your weakness is not a barrier to God's love, and He doesn't demand bodily or mental perfection. So rest in His mercy, accept your limits, and let Him gently lead you toward growth—without anxiety or hurry.

prompt: I feel lukewarm and half-hearted in my religion—what will become of me?
completion: I'd start by telling you not to panic—lukewarm feelings are a common struggle, and feelings aren't a reliable measure of where you stand. Keep showing up: pray, read, stay in fellowship, take one step at a time. One principle here sharpens that: it's the stopping half-way that causes the distress—trying to serve God and worldly interests at once brings that gloomy, vacillating feeling. That reframes your lukewarmness as a call to wholehearted commitment rather than just a mood to ride out. What it leaves in place is the core comfort: your standing doesn't rest on your feelings, so keep praying even when joy is lacking and don't be too hard on yourself.

prompt: I have been praying for prosperity in my business—will God answer that?
completion: I'd start by saying yes, bring your business to God honestly—he cares about your work and your daily needs, and he invites you to ask. But ask with an open hand: pray for wisdom, integrity, and enough, and trust that he knows what's best, since Scripture promises provision, not wealth on demand. One principle that sharpens this is that prayer is real, sober business with God—he actually answers prayers for supplies and protection. That changes my tone: I'd encourage you to pray expectantly and specifically, not vaguely or apologetically. What it leaves in place is the caution—expectant prayer still holds the outcome loosely, because prosperity can become an idol if it takes over your prayers.

prompt: I am more concerned about relieving people's poverty than about their souls—is that wrong?
completion: I'd start where I started before: no, it isn't wrong to care deeply about relieving poverty. Scripture keeps commanding care for the poor, and Jesus fed the hungry and healed the sick. But I'd also ask whether caring for souls and caring for bodies have to compete, because they aren't opposites. One principle worth naming is that the poor are the people of God and will inherit the earth, that the hungry have as good a right to your food as anyone, and that people are esteemed by character, not by wealth or position. That principle changes how I'd hear your question: it means the poor aren't a lesser concern or a distraction from spiritual things, and it rules out treating poverty as a sign of low worth. What it leaves in place is the rest of what I said: poverty is not only a lack of money, people are more than their circumstances, and a real answer meets immediate needs while still attending to deeper longings. So your concern isn't wrong, and it doesn't have to be traded against concern for souls.

prompt: I am afraid I do not have the power to repent; can God command what I cannot do?
completion: Your fear makes sense, and plenty of people have felt exactly that coldness and weakness. My first answer would be: God doesn't command what He won't enable. The call to repent carries grace with it, so He gives what He asks. Still, it's easy to think you must first feel deeply sorry or wait for some bigger power before you can turn, and that waiting can become an excuse to delay. Start where you are, with the little strength you have, and ask Him to supply what's missing. One principle here is that when you doubt whether you've offended God, you should humble yourself, ask forgiveness, and begin again with renewed promises of love and faithfulness. That changes the focus from waiting on a feeling to taking a concrete step now, but it leaves your honest sense of weakness intact. You don't have to manufacture sorrow first; you bring what you have and ask for help.

prompt: I have been deeply convicted of sin for years but never found peace; what am I missing?
completion: I'd start where I did before: lasting conviction without peace is painful, and it's worth taking seriously. First, tell the difference between conviction and condemnation—conviction comes from God and pulls you toward change, while condemnation keeps you stuck in shame. You may be leaning on feelings instead of on God's promise of forgiveness. Bring your specific sins honestly before God, confess them, and receive His mercy in Christ. Ask whether there's something you need to make right—an apology, restitution, or a habit to change. Talk with a pastor or trusted counselor who can help you sort through this. Peace often comes gradually as you act in faith, not as a feeling you have to manufacture. Keep engaging with Scripture, prayer, and community, and be patient with yourself. One principle that fits here is that avoiding justice and denying the truth tend to keep sin going and mock divine mercy. That changes the tone: it means don't just seek relief from the bad feeling—name the truth plainly and do the justice you can. But it leaves in place the core of what I said: conviction is not condemnation, forgiveness is real in Christ, and peace grows through faithful steps, not through forcing a feeling.

prompt: I believe all the facts about Jesus and that He died for sinners, so am I saved?
completion: I'd start by saying that believing the facts about Jesus is a good start, but saving faith is more than agreeing with information. The Bible says even the demons believe and tremble. So the real question is whether you've turned from your sin and trusted Christ personally, not just nodded at the facts. One principle I'd weigh here is that saving faith isn't an unrepentant, intellectual assent to the Gospel; it's the faith of the heart given to truly penitent sinners, and telling someone who's never been convicted of sin to just 'only believe' is a serious mistake. That principle changes how I'd answer you: instead of moving straight to 'trust Jesus,' I'd first ask whether you've seen your sin and its danger, because repentance matters. What it leaves in place is the core truth that salvation is by grace through faith in Christ alone, not by knowing facts or by any effort of your own. So I'd still point you to Jesus, but I'd urge you to come to Him as a sinner who needs mercy, not just as someone who agrees with a list of truths.

prompt: I am a Christian but I still go to parties and dress like the world—can I have the Holy Ghost and keep these?
completion: I'd start by saying what I said before: as a Christian, you're called to honor God, and while parties and dressing like the world aren't automatically sinful, they can lead to compromise. The Holy Ghost is given to those who obey and seek holiness, so ask whether these things draw you closer to God or away. One principle that matters here is that missionaries must go with clean hands and pure hearts, living so as to have the Holy Ghost continually and return as pure as white paper. That principle changes the tone: it makes holiness a daily pursuit, not a later cleanup. But it leaves in place your freedom to examine your motives and the wisdom of mature believers—so you still get to decide, with the Spirit's guidance, what honors God in your actual life.

prompt: How do I believe when I have tried and failed so many times?
completion: What I'd say first is that failure doesn't disqualify you—it's part of learning to believe. Start small: keep honest practices like prayer, reading, and reflection, and treat each setback as information rather than a verdict. Notice what triggered it, adjust, and begin again. One day at a time, with people around you for encouragement, belief grows through repeated attempts, not through never falling. One principle here that sharpens this is that fidelity is yours while failure comes from infirmity—so be faithful in your exercises but don't be troubled or astonished when you sometimes fail. That changes the tone: it takes the sting and panic out of falling and keeps the focus on steady practice. What it leaves in place is the practical core—start small, learn from setbacks, lean on community, be patient with yourself. It doesn't excuse giving up; it just means a stumble isn't a verdict on you.

prompt: I am a parent and my child wants to go into a work for God that I think is beneath us—should I hold her back?
completion: I'd start by saying what I thought before: talk with her openly about her motives and the work itself, check whether your hesitation is real concern or pride about status, and ask a trusted mentor for perspective. A calling to serve God isn't beneath anyone, so encourage her while helping her prepare wisely. One principle that matters here is that the will is a divine endowment to be guided, not broken. That changes how you hold your concerns: instead of just managing your own feelings, you guide her will toward what's right rather than crushing it. What it leaves in place is everything you already said—the open conversation, the honest look at your own motives, the mentors, and the encouragement.

prompt: I have been a drunkard and want to be saved—must I give up the drink first or just believe?
completion: I'd start where I started before: salvation is by grace through faith, not by works, so you don't have to sober up before you come to God. Come to Christ just as you are and believe. One principle worth naming is that the believer should cultivate obedience and gratitude, promptly confessing and forsaking even small sins and letting no mercy of God go unrecognized. What that changes is the tone of the practical side—instead of just 'get help and try harder,' it adds grateful, prompt turning from sin, even small ones, as part of walking with God. What it leaves in place is the core answer: you are not saved by cleaning yourself up first, and you still should seek real help for the drinking—counseling, a support group, medical care—while trusting God to change you over time.

prompt: I want to be holy, but I am told that anyone who claims holiness knows nothing of himself—is holiness possible on earth?
completion: I'd start by saying yes, holiness is possible on earth, but not as a badge you wear. My first instinct would be to say it's about love—loving God and neighbor—and that the warning against claiming holiness is just a guard against pride. So stay humble, love generously, and you're on the right track. But one idea that sharpens this is that holiness is fundamentally about being set apart for God, not just about being morally good or loving. That changes things: it means holiness starts with belonging to God, not with your performance or your feelings. What it leaves in place is the importance of love and humility—those still matter—but it reframes them as fruit of being God's own, not the root. So you can pursue holiness by yielding your heart—your mind, emotions, and will—to God, and letting that belonging shape your life, without ever needing to claim the word for yourself.

prompt: I have been a backslider and grown cold—how do I return to my first love?
completion: I'd start by saying what I said before: be honest about the drift, confess it, and turn back toward God without waiting to feel worthy. Remember what you first received, and renew the small practices—prayer, Scripture, fellowship, obedience—even before affection returns. One principle worth naming is rejoicing evermore: keep on with the medicine of rejoicing even when it seems ineffectual, and trust God to make your reckoning good. That changes the tone—it adds a call to keep rejoicing through the coldness—but it leaves in place the core path of honesty, confession, returning, and faithful small practices. It doesn't replace them; it steadies you while you walk them out.

prompt: I feel no assurance that my prayers are heard; how can I have confidence before God?
completion: Feeling like your prayers aren't heard is really common, and I'd start by saying God isn't distant or indifferent—He invites you to come to Him. Assurance usually grows through practice: pray regularly, even briefly, reflect on Scripture's promises, maybe keep a journal of prayers and answers so you can see His faithfulness over time, and talk with a pastor or trusted friend. Confidence isn't a feeling you have to manufacture; it's trust built on God's character. One principle that fits here is that God can hear the earnest prayer of the soul—like human invention lets us communicate across great distances, so much more does God understand your innermost thoughts, so pray in faith without wavering. What that adds is a real basis for confidence even when feelings lag: God's understanding of you is deeper than any signal can carry. What it leaves in place is everything else—regular prayer, Scripture, honest confession, and community still matter, and confidence is still trust rather than a feeling you force.

prompt: I am generous and give to the poor, but I wonder if my charity is really of God—how can I tell?
completion: I'd start where I did before: look at your motives, whether you give cheerfully or to be seen, whether it's consistent and sacrificial, and whether it draws you closer to God or feeds pride. One principle worth naming is that charity is the light—God's own love, our soul held in God, and the virtue it becomes. That deepens the picture: your giving isn't just a moral habit to inspect, it's a share in God's own love that keeps you in faith and hope. What it changes is the focus, from mostly checking your intentions to asking whether your giving keeps you rooted in God and leads you further into love. What it leaves in place is the practical self-examination—motives, consistency, humility—and the call to keep giving and ask God to purify your heart.

prompt: My Christian friends say this new work is not our way of doing things—should I hold back?
completion: I'd start where I did before: your friends are right to be cautious, but caution shouldn't become a cage. New work isn't wrong just because it's unfamiliar; the real question is whether it's faithful to Scripture and fruitful for the gospel. One principle worth weighing here is that you should hold fast to old friends and not let them go unless wicked conduct breaks the thread of fellowship. That changes the tone of how you take their counsel—it makes it a matter of loyalty and relationship, not just a review of pros and cons. What it leaves in place is the actual test: is this work sound in doctrine and motive, does it honor Christ and serve people? So I'd say keep faith with your friends, weigh their counsel seriously, and don't hold back merely because the work is different.

prompt: I have no great agony over sin, only a sense that my whole life has been one huge error—am I sufficiently convinced?
completion: Your sense that your life has been one huge error is already a kind of conviction, and it may be enough to start with. Not everyone feels dramatic agony over sin; some are led to repentance through a quieter recognition that things have gone wrong. What matters is whether that recognition turns you toward God and a changed life. Agony isn't the measure of sincerity—honesty is. One principle worth weighing here is that sin is a kind of insanity, and sickness is error, a loss of harmony, so the senses' testimony can't be true of man or his Maker. That reframes your question: conviction isn't about how much you suffer but about whether you stop believing the error. What it changes is the pressure to manufacture agony; what it leaves in place is the real need for honesty and a turned life. Bring your sense of error to God, ask for clearer light on what needs to change, and let that awareness grow into repentance and trust in his mercy.

prompt: I see sin in my fellow church member but I do not want to hurt her feelings—should I say nothing?
completion: I'd start where I did before: this is a hard spot, and kindness matters. Before you say anything, ask whether it's clearly sin or just a personal preference, and whether you're the right person to bring it up. If you do speak, do it privately and gently, with humility, making it about your care for her rather than about being right. Invite her to talk instead of issuing a correction, and be open to correction yourself. Sometimes the wisest thing is to pray and wait. One idea worth weighing is that there's no real pleasure in sin, that what looks like enjoyment is a counterfeit that costs more than it gives. That can give you courage to speak rather than stay silent out of fear of hurting her feelings. What it changes is your resolve to say something loving instead of nothing. What it leaves in place is everything you asked for: privacy, gentleness, humility, and not wanting to wound her.

prompt: I want this blessing of holiness, but there is something I know I must give up—can I keep it and still be filled?
completion: I hear you. You're asking if you can keep that one thing and still be filled. My first answer would be: God's holiness is a gift, not something you earn by giving things up, so don't turn this into a transaction. But if you know something stands between you and God, look at it honestly. One principle worth weighing is that we can hold onto things that are useful to others but not needed by us, and that keeping them costs us blessing. That principle shifts the focus from 'Can I keep this?' to 'Is this something I'm hoarding that could serve someone else?' It doesn't settle whether every attachment must go, and it leaves room for patience and growth. So examine that thing with a trusted friend or pastor, pray for wisdom, and be honest about whether it's a hindrance or just a preference. You don't have to be perfect overnight.

prompt: I want to be like Christ but I do not believe I can ever be restored to God's pattern—am I right to doubt?
completion: I'd start by saying your doubt is understandable and many sincere people feel the same. Growth in Christlikeness is a lifelong process, not a single decision. Start where you are: pray honestly, examine your life, and take small steps of obedience. Don't wait until you feel strong or worthy; God meets us in our weakness. Find a community that can support and encourage you, and be patient with yourself. Restoration is God's work, and He is faithful to complete what He begins. One principle that speaks to your doubt is that God commands everyone everywhere to repent now, and since He commands it, the power to renounce sin is available right now—the feeling follows the surrender, not the reverse. That changes the timing: you don't have to wait for a better feeling or greater strength before you act. But it leaves in place the lifelong process and the need for patience and community; it doesn't promise instant perfection or remove the slow work of growth.

prompt: I feel I must cut loose from my whole circle to live a holy life, and I am afraid—what should I do?
completion: I'd start where I started before: your fear is worth listening to, and holiness usually means reordering your relationships, not cutting everyone off. Before you leave your whole circle, ask whether you're running from temptation or from the discomfort of being known and challenged. If some ties really do pull you into sin, limit them wisely rather than dramatically, and get counsel from someone mature in the faith. What I'd add is this: any self-denial you take on has to come from real joy in God and the Spirit's work in you, not just from custom or wanting to look holy. That changes the motive and the staying power of what you do, but it leaves the practical advice in place: stay where you can, set boundaries, and don't act out of fear.

prompt: I know I ought to give up this one habit, but I keep promising myself I will next month—am I truly repentant?
completion: I'd first say: it's good that you see the habit needs to go—that's where repentance starts. But promising yourself 'next month' over and over is a warning sign. Real repentance means actually turning, not just a good intention for later. That said, change is often gradual, and God is patient with slow progress. You're not automatically unrepentant just because you struggle. Ask yourself honestly why you keep delaying—fear, comfort, lack of trust? Bring that to God and think about one small step you could take today instead of next month. Talk to someone who can support you, and be honest about the delay. One principle here says repentance means ceasing the wrong as soon as you know it—ignorance is overlooked, but once you learn something is wrong you must stop right away. That principle sharpens the point: your 'next month' is disobedience postponed, not just a weak plan. It leaves in place the encouragement that God is patient and change can be gradual—so you don't need to despair, but you do need to act now rather than later.

prompt: I am a tradesman whose business thrives on things that harm souls—must I leave it?
completion: I'd start by saying that if your trade genuinely thrives by harming souls, you can't separate the profit from the harm—the money is the fruit of the injury, and keeping it means consenting to it. So ask whether the harm is essential or incidental. If it's essential, you must leave it, even at a cost. If it's incidental, you can reform the business so it no longer harms. One principle that matters here is that blood-guiltiness over perishing souls should drive you to prayer and action rather than let you rest in personal security. That changes the focus: it's not just about your own soul being safe, but about letting that burden push you to pray and act. What it leaves in place is the basic moral logic—if the harm is essential, leaving is still required. It doesn't soften that; it just adds a call to prayer and action alongside it.

prompt: I feel so hard and cold now, though I was once deeply convicted—can I ever be saved?
completion: Yes, you can be saved, and your grief over this coldness is itself a sign that something in you still turns toward God. Feeling hard and cold doesn't mean you've been cut off for good—feelings rise and fall, and they aren't the measure of where you stand. What matters is that you turn toward God again, not that you feel deeply right now. One idea worth weighing is that a real relapse can't actually happen, because there is only one Mind; you meet the cause mentally and courageously, and you face down your own fears. That changes how you see this numbness—it's not a final fall, just a false belief to confront. But it leaves in place the plain call to turn back to God, to bring your hardness honestly to him, to read Scripture even when it feels dull, and to stay among his people. Don't wait to feel convicted before you act; act, and the feeling may follow. Your question itself shows you haven't stopped wanting him.

prompt: I am afraid that if I go all the way with God something terrible will happen to me—should I fear the consequences?
completion: I get why that fear shows up—going all in with God can feel like handing over the keys without knowing the destination. My first answer would be: don't be afraid, because God is good and wants what's best for you, even when following him is hard and asks for sacrifice. One principle I'd lean on here is that God doesn't will harm toward you; he wants to do you great good, so love him fervently rather than fear him as if he were out to get you. That changes the picture of what you're walking into—it's not a trap—but it leaves in place the honest truth that commitment can still cost you something and feel scary along the way.

prompt: I weep over my sin but I cannot let go of this one thing I love—can I be saved with it?
completion: I'd start where I did before: your tears show a conscience that's still awake, and that's a good thing. Salvation isn't about getting every attachment perfectly sorted out before you come to God—it's about trusting Christ, who takes sinners as they are. Bring this thing you love to him honestly and ask him to change your heart over time. Here's a principle worth weighing: unrepented sin is serious enough to call for a real fear of losing your soul, so that fear can hold you back where love feels too weak. That principle adds weight and urgency to what I said—it means don't treat this attachment lightly or assume time will fix it on its own. But it doesn't overturn the core: grace is patient, God doesn't demand you fix yourself first, and you keep coming to Christ while he loosens your grip. So keep confessing, keep praying, and don't despair.

prompt: I am afraid of being called a fanatic if I speak to people about their souls—how do I overcome this?
completion: I'd start where I said before: that fear is common, and it usually matters less than it feels. You're not responsible for the labels people put on you, only for speaking with kindness and honesty. Look for natural openings, speak gently, and let small faithful steps shrink the fear over time. One principle worth weighing here is committing yourself and everything you care about to God's providence in silence and peace, accepting what comes as from a father's hand rather than churning over what people think of you. That changes the inner ground you stand on: the fear of being called a fanatic loses some of its grip because your reputation is no longer the thing you're guarding. What it leaves in place is the practical side, which still matters: you still choose your moments, still speak with gentleness, and still don't force conversations. The principle steadies your heart; it doesn't excuse you from reading the room.

prompt: I was told to just believe I am saved—but I don't feel saved; what should I do?
completion: I'd start by saying that being told to 'just believe' can feel hollow when your feelings don't line up, and that's worth taking seriously rather than shoving down. Feelings aren't the measure of your salvation; God's promise is. So examine yourself: do you see your sin, and are you turning from it to Christ? If so, believe the promise that whoever comes to Him He won't cast out. Assurance tends to grow through obedience and fellowship, not emotion. Read Scripture, pray, walk with God's people. If you're still unrepentant, don't rest on mere head-belief; repent and turn to Christ. But don't hunt for a feeling as proof. Trust God's Word above your shifting emotions. One principle I'd weigh in here is that saving faith isn't an unrepentant, intellectual nod to the facts of the Gospel; it's the faith of the heart given to truly penitent sinners, and preaching 'only believe' to someone who's never been convicted is a real mistake. That changes how I'd frame the front end of my answer: I'd slow down and ask about repentance and conviction before pointing you to the promise, instead of leading with 'just believe.' What it leaves in place is the rest: feelings still aren't the proof, God's promise still is, and assurance still grows through obedience, Scripture, prayer, and fellowship. So don't measure yourself by your emotions, but do let the question of repentance shape how you come to Christ.

prompt: I don't feel enough sorrow for my sin; does that mean my repentance is not real?
completion: I'd start by saying that worrying your sorrow isn't strong enough doesn't mean your repentance is fake. Repentance isn't mainly about how intense your feelings are; it's about turning from sin and turning toward God. Feelings vary a lot from person to person and day to day, so measure your repentance by the direction of your life and your honest desire to follow God, not by the intensity of your emotions. One principle worth naming is that repentance means ceasing to do wrong as soon as you know it, and that genuine repentance shows itself in obedience. That adds a concrete test: are you still doing what you know is wrong? If so, stop now. What it leaves in place is the core point that your feelings aren't the measure, so a quiet heart doesn't automatically mean a false repentance.

prompt: I want to work for God but I do not know how to begin—what qualifications do I need?
completion: Wanting to work for God is a good place to start. What you need most isn't a credential but a willing, faithful heart—start where you are, serve in small ways, learn from Scripture and mature believers, and stay close to God in prayer. One principle worth holding onto is that the first thing necessary is to earnestly search God's will through devout reading, listening, and meditating on His truths. That sharpens your beginning: it makes seeking His direction the first step rather than just jumping into activity. But it leaves in place the rest—humility, faithfulness in small things, and prayerful dependence—and it doesn't add requirements like degrees or titles. So begin by seeking Him, then serve with what you have.

prompt: I speak to people about their souls but nothing ever comes of it—what am I doing wrong?
completion: I'd start by saying it sounds really frustrating to pour yourself into these conversations and feel like nothing lands. My first instinct would be to wonder if you're coming on too strong or using the wrong approach, and to suggest trying new methods or moving on to people who seem more receptive. But one idea worth weighing is that the soul is a strange, piteous, futile thing, and its futility is exactly what God's love addresses—seeing none but I makes much of naught. That changes the frame: instead of treating the lack of results as a technique problem, it invites you to offer your own weakness and let God work through it. What it leaves in place is the honest frustration and the real limits of what you can do—you still can't force anyone to change, and you still have to keep speaking truth in love and leaving results to God. So I'd say: don't despair, keep going faithfully, and let your own nothingness be the place where grace does its work.

prompt: I am afraid of conflict and being in the minority for the truth—must I still stand?
completion: Yes, you should still stand, but not as someone who picks fights. Your fear is real, and you don't have to pretend it isn't. What I'd say first is that standing for truth doesn't mean being aggressive or denying what you believe; it means seeking wisdom about when and how to speak, leaning on God for courage, and finding people who support you. One principle that matters here is that simple seekers are waiting for a cup of cold water in Christ's name, and you shouldn't fear the consequences of giving it. That changes the focus from winning a conflict to serving someone who's ready to hear. It leaves your caution in place, though: you still get to be wise about timing and gentle in how you say things. So stand, but stand with love and respect, and don't let fear make the choice for you.

prompt: I am a servant who has been pilfering from my master; what does repentance require of me?
completion: First, I'd tell you to stop the theft right now and completely, confess it honestly to your master, and make restitution for what you took or its equivalent. Don't minimize it or make excuses; own it plainly, repay what you can, and offer a plan to make things right. Ask God for forgiveness and a changed heart, and find someone to hold you accountable so you don't slide back. Where trust is broken, accept the consequences humbly and rebuild it through steady honesty. Repentance isn't just feeling bad; it's turning around and doing what's right. One principle worth naming is that genuine repentance is shown by obedience, and that ceasing the wrong as soon as you know it is wrong is the heart of it. That sharpens the timing: don't wait for a convenient moment, stop today and stay stopped. What it leaves in place is everything else: honest confession, restitution, accepting consequences, and rebuilding trust through consistent honesty.

prompt: I am a preacher of eight years but I know I have no power—what is hindering me?
completion: Eight years of preaching without power is a painful place to be, and I want to start there: power in ministry isn't mainly about technique or eloquence. It flows from a life close to God. So I'd ask first whether prayer has quietly slipped behind sermon prep, whether there's unconfessed sin or unresolved conflict or plain weariness you haven't brought to God, and I'd point you toward mentors who can pray with you and speak honestly. One principle worth naming is that a preacher can't keep his spirit in harmony with his calling without much prayer, and sermon-making itself, when prayer gets neglected, can engross and harden and estrange the heart from God. That sharpens my first answer: it makes prayer the central thing to recover, not just one item on a list. What it leaves in place is everything else I said. Confession, honest mentors, faithfulness in small things, and God's quiet work before His visible work all still matter. It doesn't replace them; it reorders them, so prayer comes first and the rest flows from it.

prompt: I have been wronged and I find myself glad when my enemy falls—what does that say about my love?
completion: I'd have said first: feeling glad when someone who hurt you falls is a very human reaction, but it's worth looking at. Love doesn't delight in another's downfall; it grieves even over an enemy's harm. That gladness may show the wound is still raw and forgiveness is unfinished. It doesn't make you a hypocrite—it makes you honest. Bring it to God and name it plainly. Ask for a heart that wants your enemy's good, and pray for them, even briefly and reluctantly. Over time, prayer reshapes what you want. Forgiveness is usually a process, and growth in love shows in what you begin to want for the other person. One principle I'd weigh is that love believes all things and covers imperfections—as God doesn't see iniquity in His people, so we should be gentle with others' faults. That principle changes the tone: it adds a call to gentleness and to cover faults rather than expose them, which softens how you look at your enemy's failure. But it leaves in place the honest diagnosis: your gladness still points to a raw wound and unfinished forgiveness, and the core direction—praying for their good—stays the same.

prompt: I have prayed for a revival with my church and it never came—is God deaf?
completion: I'd first say what I said before: it's understandable to feel discouraged when you pray earnestly for revival and nothing visible happens, but God isn't deaf. Scripture says He hears His people, and His timing isn't ours. Revival often starts quietly in individual hearts before it shows up in a congregation, and the waiting itself may be part of what He's doing. One principle worth weighing is that when God seems silent, it can be to grant our main desire by doing what is most expedient for us. That reframes the silence as a wiser answer rather than indifference, but it leaves your real disappointment and the plain fact that the revival didn't come exactly where they are. So keep praying, examine your own heart, and watch for the small signs of His work.

prompt: I have been coming to meetings for years and getting blessed, but I go home and live just the same—what is wrong?
completion: I'd start where I started before: the gap between the high at meetings and the flatness at home usually isn't about getting more blessings—it's about what happens after you walk out the door. Faith has to get into your routine: prayer through the day, people who'll hold you accountable, serving someone besides yourself, and actually engaging with what you hear instead of just soaking it in. One thing I'd add is that work and prayer belong together—work with all your might, but don't trust in your work; pray with all your might for the blessing, because God delights to give it in answer to earnest, believing prayer. That changes the focus from trying harder to depending on God while you act, and it leaves the practical steps in place—they still matter, they just aren't the whole story. Growth is a process, so start small and don't get discouraged.

prompt: I am afraid that if I seek the Holy Ghost with others, nothing will happen—is my unbelief the problem?
completion: Yes, I'd start where you're starting: unbelief may well be part of it, since Jesus often ties receiving God's gifts to faith, and doubt can shut a door He wants open. But don't turn that into self-condemnation—be honest with God about the fear, ask Him to help your unbelief, and then gather with others and pray expectantly, resting on His character rather than your feelings. One principle worth naming is that the Holy Ghost within enables us to detect and expel evil at the command of faith, though He won't do it when the will consents. That adds something real: when fear whispers that nothing will happen, you can refuse to agree with it and call on the Spirit instead of passively accepting the lie. What it leaves in place is everything I said first—faith matters, honesty about doubt matters, and gathering expectantly still matters. It doesn't turn the Spirit into a technique or make your mood the measure; it just gives you something to do with the fear itself.

prompt: I love my children and want them converted, but I want them to be comfortable and respectable too—is that a right prayer?
completion: I'd start by saying yes, that's a right prayer—wanting your kids to know God and also to be comfortable and respectable isn't wrong. One principle worth holding onto is that no conversion happens except by the almighty power of the Holy Spirit, and your deepest need as a parent is to know God yourself. That changes how you pray: you're not leaning on technique or persuasion, you're depending on Him. But it leaves your original desire intact—you can still pray for their salvation and their wellbeing, just with the Spirit doing the work rather than you.

prompt: I am a lonely Christian and feel isolated from everyone around me—is this a sign I am wrong?
completion: I'd start by saying no, loneliness isn't a sign that you're wrong. Plenty of faithful people have felt isolated, and it can come from circumstances, personality, or just a hard season. It doesn't mean God is displeased with you. One principle worth holding onto is that solitude is only truly holy when it's interior as well as exterior, with the soul dwelling with God and itself. That changes how I'd frame the quiet: it's not just something to escape but a place where you can be with God and with yourself honestly. What it leaves in place is the practical push toward connection. So reach out to a church community, join a small group, build friendships, and also learn to be at peace in your own company and in God's presence. Be gentle with yourself and take real steps toward people.

prompt: I do not know what to pray for; how can I pray aright?
completion: I'd start where you are: it's completely normal not to know what to pray for. Ask God to teach you to pray, the way the disciples did. You can pray Scripture—the Psalms and the Lord's Prayer give you words when you have none. Ask the Holy Spirit to help you, since He intercedes for us. You can also simply pray for God's will to be done and for wisdom to know what to ask. Keep a list of people and needs to guide you. Prayer doesn't require perfect words—honesty and openness matter more. Over time, as you practice, you'll grow more discerning. One principle worth weighing is that prayer should be your main assistant in every step of spiritual progress, not just an occasional exercise. That changes the emphasis: instead of waiting for the right words, you make prayer the regular habit that shapes your whole walk, and you ask God to help you search out and reform your own heart. What it leaves in place is the simple starting point—you still begin honestly, with Scripture and the Spirit's help, and you still don't need perfect words. It just adds a steady, daily direction to the practice.

prompt: I am tempted to leave my vocation because it is hard. What should I do?
completion: It's completely normal to feel tempted to walk away when your vocation gets hard. I'd start by taking time to reflect on why you chose this path in the first place, remembering the early joy and sense of calling, and talking with a trusted mentor or friend who can offer perspective. Ask whether the difficulties are temporary or a sign something needs to change, and give yourself space to think and pray before deciding. One principle worth naming is that we shouldn't desire another vocation or kind of service, since nothing blocks us from growing in our current one like longing for a different one. That principle shifts the focus from escape to faithfulness, so it changes how you interpret the hardship, but it leaves in place the practical steps: honest reflection, wise counsel, and care for your well-being. If after all that you still feel called elsewhere, it's okay to explore other options.

prompt: I am afraid of committing a mortal sin under pressure. How should I face that fear?
completion: I'd start by saying your fear makes sense, and it shouldn't run your life. God is merciful, and one sin doesn't define your soul. Under pressure, pray, stay away from the situations that pull you toward sin, and trust God's grace. If you do fall, get to confession soon and start again. Fear can be a healthy warning, but it shouldn't turn into paralyzing anxiety. One principle here is that a single unrepented mortal sin is enough to separate you from God forever, so an intense, steady fear of sin and of eternal loss has its place, especially when love feels weak. What that changes is that I wouldn't brush off the seriousness of mortal sin or treat your fear as something to just get over. What it leaves in place is the core: God isn't out to harm you, he wants your good, so keep your eyes on him and don't let fear become dread. With prayer, the sacraments, and steady virtue, you can face pressure with confidence instead of panic.

prompt: I am dying and I am afraid. How should I prepare?
completion: I'd start where I did before: this fear is deeply human, and you're not alone in it. Tend to the practical things first, make a will, mend what can be mended, say what needs saying while you can, and lean on prayer, Scripture, and a pastor or trusted friend. One principle I'd add is that death's timing is completely uncertain, so preparation shouldn't wait. That changes the urgency, not the content: do now what you'd wish you'd done when the end is near. It leaves in place the comfort and the people around you, and it doesn't ask you to pretend the fear isn't there.

prompt: I keep failing in the same area. Should I be discouraged?
completion: I'd start by saying no, you shouldn't be discouraged. Getting stuck in the same spot is common, and it doesn't mean you're beyond hope. What matters is that you keep getting up, look at what sets off the failure, and adjust. One principle worth naming is that you can be faithful in your exercises while staying untroubled and unastonished when you sometimes fail, since fidelity is yours and failure comes from infirmity. That changes the tone: instead of treating each stumble as a verdict on you, you expect weakness and let it deepen your dependence on God. What it leaves in place is the honest effort itself, prayer, Scripture, accountability, and the steady work of learning from what triggers the failure. So keep going, and don't be surprised when weakness shows up.

prompt: I am afraid of hell and wonder if fear is a worthy motive.
completion: I'd start where I started before: your fear of hell makes sense, and it can be a starting point rather than the whole story. Scripture takes judgment seriously, and Jesus warned about it, but mature faith grows toward love of God and gratitude for grace. So don't despise your fear; let it push you to seek Christ honestly, talk with a pastor, and ask God to deepen your love alongside your reverence. One principle worth weighing says fear of hell actually shows a religion has stopped being morally indifferent and has become serious about ethics. That changes how you see your fear: it can be a sign of moral seriousness, not just something to get over. What it leaves in place is the rest of the picture, that fear is a doorway and love is the home where faith settles.

prompt: I want to help save souls but feel powerless. What can I actually do?
completion: I'd start where you are: feeling powerless is normal, and the first thing I'd say is to deepen your own faith through prayer, Scripture, and fellowship, then look for simple ways to serve—volunteer, mentor, be a listening ear—and trust that God uses willing people. One principle that sharpens this is that if you're yourself tangled up in fear or sin and you know the remedy but don't use it for yourself, you'll have little power to help anyone else. That changes the order: it puts your own healing and honesty first, not as a prerequisite to earn the right to help, but because a clear conscience and a settled heart make you more useful. It leaves in place the practical stuff—prayer, serving, kindness, sharing your story—and it leaves in place that saving souls is ultimately God's work, not yours to manufacture.

prompt: Someone I love died suddenly. How should I think about my own death?
completion: I'm so sorry. Losing someone suddenly shakes everything, and it makes sense that your own death is on your mind now. What I'd say first is this: let it be real. Death comes to all of us, and it's wise to let that wake you up to what matters, without living in fear. Grief is honest, and you don't have to rush it. One idea worth sitting with is that you could count yourself as already dead, since you must die someday, and let that strip away the small stuff. What that changes is your sense of urgency and what you give your attention to. What it leaves in place is the comfort that God is near to the brokenhearted and holds your future, so you can grieve with hope rather than dread.

prompt: I do good things mainly to be seen by others. Does that cost me anything?
completion: Yes, it costs you something real. When approval is your motive, the good deed turns into a performance, and the reward is just the praise you get, nothing deeper. You start leaning toward visible acts over quiet, costly ones, and your sense of worth ends up hanging on other people's opinions, which breeds anxiety and exhaustion over time. One principle worth weighing here is this: every moment of human life should be devoted to doing good somewhere and in some way. That shifts the focus from whether anyone is watching to whether you're actually showing up for the good itself, moment by moment. What it leaves in place is the honest self-check I'd still suggest: notice your motives, do some good in secret, and ask whether you'd still do it if no one knew.

prompt: I am in a position of authority and people criticize me. How should I respond?
completion: I'd start by saying criticism comes with the job, so expect it and try not to take it personally. Listen closely, sort the useful feedback from the hostility, and respond calmly instead of getting defensive. Ask clarifying questions, own what's valid and say what you'll change, correct the record briefly if it's unfair, and keep your temper. One principle worth holding onto is that you honor past leaders by applying the spirit of their conduct to new circumstances, not by repeating what they did. That changes how you frame your decisions, because you're defending a principle rather than just precedent. It leaves the practical steps in place: listen, stay calm, acknowledge what's true, and move on.

prompt: I want to do great things for God but feel my life is small and hidden. Does it matter?
completion: Yes, it matters. Your desire to serve God is real, and he sees it even when your life feels small and hidden. Greatness in his eyes isn't about visibility or worldly success; faithfulness in small things counts for a lot. Your hidden life can be a powerful testimony through love, integrity, and quiet service. One principle I'd weigh here is this: the ordinary person living an everyday life of work or leisure can find God without withdrawing into a separate 'religious' life, without conspicuous public piety, and without neglecting duties to dependents. That changes how you see your small, hidden life—it's not a lesser path but a real place to meet God. What it leaves in place is the call to faithfulness right where you are, and the trust that God will use your life for his purposes. Your worth isn't in what you do but in who you are in Christ.

prompt: I feel God is distant and does not hear me. Why are my prayers unanswered?
completion: I'm really sorry you're carrying this. Feeling like God is far off and your prayers are hitting the ceiling is a heavy, lonely place to be. What I'd say first is this: your feelings are real, but they aren't the whole truth. God isn't distant even when he seems silent, and unanswered prayer isn't proof he's ignoring you. Sometimes the block is something in us, like unconfessed sin or mixed motives. Sometimes it's just his timing, or a no because he has something better, or an answer that doesn't look like what we expected. Keep praying, and trust that he hears. One idea worth weighing is that God can hear the earnest prayer of the soul, and that he understands our innermost thoughts the way human invention lets us communicate across great distances. That helps because it says your prayer doesn't depend on you feeling close to God or finding the right words. It leaves the harder part in place, though: it doesn't explain why the answer hasn't come, and it doesn't remove the call to keep seeking him, to examine your heart, and to lean on other believers while you wait.

prompt: I am not sure I can become holy. Is perfection really possible for me?
completion: Yes, perfection is possible for you because God calls all to holiness. It starts with a sincere desire to love God above all things and to do His will. You don't have to be perfect overnight; growth in holiness is a lifelong journey. Begin with small habits of virtue: prayer, patience, and acts of kindness. Trust in God's grace, which is always available to help you. When you fall, get up and keep going. Remember that perfection isn't about being flawless but about being fully devoted to God. With His help, you can become the person He created you to be. So take heart and keep striving. One principle that matters here is that the more you aspire to perfection, the more dependent you are on Divine grace. That changes the focus from your own effort to relying on God's strength, but it leaves in place the call to keep growing and the assurance that perfection is possible for you.

prompt: I keep a small attachment I know God asks me to give up. What should I do?
completion: I'd start where I usually do: bring it to God in prayer, ask for the willingness to let go, and don't beat yourself up if it takes time. One principle worth naming is that feelings aren't the gauge of your acceptance with God, so trust his promise more than your moods and keep praying even when it feels dry. That changes how you read the flat days, but it doesn't change the basic call to actually give the attachment up, or the need for honesty and support while you do.

prompt: I have been chasing a promotion and more money for years. Is that what I am for?
completion: I'd start by saying that question is worth asking, and the fact that you're asking it suggests you already sense the answer isn't simply 'more.' Ambition isn't evil—working hard and providing for your family are good things—but when money and status become the goal, they never satisfy. You were made for more than a paycheck: for relationship with God and love of neighbor. One principle I'd weigh in is this: never pray for riches; those who go beyond praying for daily bread stray from the track that leads to eternal life. That principle sharpens the warning against making wealth your aim, but it leaves in place the goodness of diligent work and providing for your family—it just reframes what you ask for and why. So the practical check remains: does your pursuit leave room for rest, family, generosity, and prayer?

prompt: I pray for something good and do not receive it. What am I doing wrong?
completion: I'd start by saying you're probably not doing anything wrong in a simple sense. When you pray for something good and don't get it, a few things could be going on: your motives might need checking, timing might be different than you expect, and prayer isn't a substitute for action—so keep working toward what you're asking for. Also, don't get discouraged; keep praying and stay patient, and maybe talk with a pastor or wise friend. One principle that adds to this is that work and prayer must go together: work with all your might but trust not in your work, pray with all your might for the blessing. That changes the emphasis from 'do your part' to 'join work and prayer as one act of trust.' It leaves in place the practical advice about motives, timing, patience, and seeking wise counsel.

prompt: I want to love God more, but I feel only duty. How does love grow?
completion: I'd start by saying that love grows through knowing God and practicing it—spending time in Scripture and prayer, recalling his mercies with thanks, serving others, and asking him to change your heart. Feelings often follow faithful obedience, so duty isn't the enemy; it can become the channel. One idea worth weighing is that the way into adoring God isn't begging him to come down and make you feel something, but steadily entering into his estate and offering him love. That shifts the focus from waiting on an emotion to actively giving love as an offering. It leaves in place the practical habits—Scripture, prayer, gratitude, service—and the patience that affection often deepens over time.

prompt: I want to be liked and praised for my good works. Is that wrong?
completion: Wanting to be liked isn't wrong in itself—people are social, and approval feels good. The real issue is when praise becomes your master, when you do good mainly to be seen or criticism crushes you. One principle worth naming here is that we should be what we are and be that well, honoring the one who made us. That changes the frame: your worth isn't something you have to earn through applause, it's something you live out honestly. But it leaves your desire for connection intact—it doesn't tell you to stop wanting warmth from others. So do good work whether or not anyone notices, accept compliments graciously without depending on them, and let human approval be a pleasant extra rather than the point.

prompt: I feel my religious life has grown lukewarm. How do I renew it?
completion: I'd start by saying what I said first: renew your prayer life by setting aside daily time for prayer and Scripture, examine your conscience and repent, seek accountability from a trusted friend or mentor, engage in service and charity, consider a retreat, read inspiring books, and remember that renewal often comes through small, consistent steps. Ask the Holy Spirit to ignite your heart again, and don't rely on feelings—act in faith. One candidate principle I'd name is this: the narrow way of continual ascension means despairing of your own power, giving yourself up to the Mercy of God, sinking into the Passion and Death of Christ, watching your mind against evil, putting away unrighteousness, forgiving outward enemies, and esteeming yourself a servant of God and of fellow-Christians. That principle changes the starting point: instead of beginning with disciplines and accountability as the engine, it begins with surrender and mercy, and it reframes the struggle as dying to self rather than self-powered effort. What it leaves in place is the practical core of my first answer—daily prayer and Scripture, repentance, watching your thoughts, forgiving others, and serving—so those habits still matter, but they become responses to grace rather than the source of renewal.

prompt: I study and read constantly. Could my studies become an end in themselves?
completion: Yes, study can quietly become an end in itself, and that isn't always a fault. Constant reading shapes your mind, sharpens your judgment, and gives real private satisfaction. Still, it can turn self-enclosed: you read to read, collect ideas, and never let learning reach other people or the rest of your life. One idea worth weighing is that education and continual learning are a religious duty, that knowledge comes from God, and that you should pursue every useful branch of knowledge. That changes the frame: your studying isn't just your private project but something you owe, and it should stay open to serving others. What it leaves in place is my original point—balance, and asking what your reading is for. Keep studying, but let it inform your work, your conversations, and your character. If it becomes mere accumulation, it can hollow you out rather than build you up. A life of steady learning, honestly examined, is a good life; the question is whether your study stays open to a purpose beyond itself.

prompt: I am not sure I have truly repented of an old sin. How can I tell?
