prompt: How can I know the doctrine is of God rather than of men?
completion: I'd start where I'd naturally start: test the teaching against Scripture, pray for discernment, look at the fruit it produces and the character of the teacher, and stay humble and patient since understanding usually comes gradually. One idea worth weighing is that God is incorporeal, infinite Love rather than a corporeal person, and that praying to a bodily God can keep us stuck in human doubts and fears. If that's true, it changes how you'd evaluate a doctrine: you'd ask whether it honors God as Spirit and corrects the belief that life and intelligence live in matter, rather than judging it by striking signs or by how well it fits a picture of God as a person located somewhere. What it leaves in place is the core of my first answer: Scripture, prayer, fruit, humility, and patience still matter. It just reframes what you're looking for when you test a teaching.

prompt: What happens to those who died without ever hearing the gospel?
completion: My first answer would be that Scripture presents God as just and merciful, and it doesn't clearly say that anyone is condemned for light they never received. The Bible doesn't give us a detailed map of what happens to the unevangelized, so I'd hold that humbly and trust God's character, while affirming that salvation is in Christ and that God wants all people saved. One idea worth weighing is that the gospel is preached to the dead, so those who never heard it may hear it in the spirit, with work for the dead carried on in temples. That changes the picture from 'we simply don't know' to 'there's a hopeful path after death.' What it leaves in place is the core conviction that Christ is the only Savior and that God is just and merciful. It doesn't settle every detail, and I'd still be careful about claiming more than we can know.

prompt: Will the earth be restored to its former glory, and what will that look like?
completion: I'd start by saying the earth's future in Scripture often looks like destruction and renewal, with the present order passing away and the righteous escaping to heaven. But one principle here changes that: the restoration of all things means the earth will be brought back to its primeval glory—one land, fruitful, without curse—and humanity restored with it. That shifts the focus from escape to healing, yet it leaves in place the idea that the present world still passes through judgment before renewal. So the renewed earth would look like Eden restored, but the old order still gives way first.

prompt: Why do Christian nations go to war with one another and pray to the same God for victory?
completion: I'd start by saying that Christian nations fight because nations, even Christian ones, are full of fallible people chasing security, power, and national interest, and when those clash, governments turn to force while churches get caught between blessing the troops and calling for peace. Praying to the same God for victory is a tragic irony, since each side thinks its cause is just. One idea that sharpens this is that war is the natural penalty by which evil passions punish themselves under God's ordinary laws of human nature, so wars grow out of lusts and injustice rather than God's design. That changes how I see the causes, making them moral and self-inflicted rather than just political, but it leaves in place the point that God doesn't take sides in the slaughter and that Christians still answer for letting patriotism crowd out the gospel's call to peacemaking.

prompt: Will I see my family and children again in the world to come?
completion: I'd start where I started before: this is one of the deepest hopes we have, and Scripture gives real ground for it. The world to come isn't a vague shadowland; it's the renewed creation where God dwells with His people, and relationships aren't erased but healed and perfected. If God cares for sparrows and numbers the hairs of our heads, He surely doesn't sever the bonds of love He Himself planted in families. One principle worth weighing is that the restoration of all things means the earth is brought back to its primeval glory and man restored with it. That changes the setting of the hope—it makes the promise earthy and concrete rather than purely otherworldly, so families and children belong within a restored order. What it leaves in place is the core comfort: the God who raised Jesus will raise us, and nothing in Christ is finally lost. So grieve honestly, but grieve with hope.

prompt: How should I live now in light of the coming kingdom of God?
completion: I'd start where I started before: live with intention, since the kingdom is near. Build habits of prayer, generosity, and integrity, take responsibility for your growth, mend relationships, and stay awake to what matters rather than passively waiting. One principle worth naming is that unless you become like a little child, hanging on Christ for everything, you can't enter the kingdom. That changes the footing of everything I just said: the habits and goals stop being a project you pull off and become a way of depending on him, so your effort rests on his grace instead of your willpower. What it leaves in place is the practical shape of the life: prayer, generosity, integrity, mending what's broken, using your gifts for others. You still act decisively; you just act as a child holding on, not as someone building a résumé.

prompt: Will God punish the world in the last days, and will he warn us first?
completion: Yes, I'd say Scripture holds out both: a real judgment at the end, and real warning before it comes. My first answer would be that God has always warned before He judges—Noah preaching while the ark went up, Lot pulled out of Sodom, prophets crying out to Jerusalem before it fell—and that pattern carries through to the last days, when God sends His Spirit and His messengers to call people to turn to Christ. One principle I'd weigh here is that it would be unjust for God to punish the ignorant without warning, so He warns first. That principle sharpens the point: the warning is genuine and meant to be heeded now, not later. What it leaves in place is that the judgment itself is still real and still coming for those who refuse—warning doesn't cancel the consequence, it gives people a way to escape it. So the question isn't whether God warns, but whether we listen while there's still time.

prompt: Can I find peace and happiness by moving to a new country with plenty of food and land?
completion: I'd start by saying that moving to a new country with plenty of food and land can bring real relief, but peace and happiness are interior realities that travel with you rather than living in a place. One principle here says this world is a touchstone and finding-place for God, and that true happiness comes from finding God from this world rather than waiting for the next. That changes the frame: the move becomes a setting for seeking something deeper, not a cure-all. It leaves in place the practical advice to think about community, legal stability, and work before you go, and it still warns that happiness isn't guaranteed by geography or abundance.

prompt: Why is chastity so important, and what are the eternal consequences of impurity?
completion: I'd start by saying chastity matters because your body and soul are made for God, and impurity throws both into disorder. Scripture is blunt that the impure won't inherit the kingdom, so the stakes really are eternal: unrepented impurity cuts you off from God, while purity of heart opens the way to seeing him. Chastity isn't just a social rule; it's a safeguard for your union with God. One principle I'd add is that chastity is a treasure you protect through prayer, self-denial, modesty of the senses, especially the eyes, and by steering clear of temptation, since whoever loves danger will perish in it. That changes the practical side of my answer: it turns a general warning into concrete habits. But it leaves the core in place: the eternal stakes and the call to guard your union with God.

prompt: What is Zion, and should I gather to it?
completion: My first answer was that Zion is a place of gathering and spiritual community, and whether you should gather depends on your circumstances—weigh family, work, finances, and avoid unhealthy groups. One candidate principle says church duties should be paramount above every other interest, with the cause of Zion uppermost in your thoughts and highest in your love. That principle changes the framing: gathering isn't just a personal choice to weigh against practical concerns; it becomes a priority that other interests should be ordered around. But it leaves in place the practical reality that you still have to work, care for family, and use judgment about any group—it doesn't erase those concerns, just reorders them.

prompt: What is the point of peace societies and congresses if war keeps breaking out anyway?
completion: My first answer would be that peace societies and congresses still matter because they keep the ideal of peace in front of the world, educate public opinion, and open channels for negotiation before conflicts escalate. War breaking out doesn't prove those efforts are useless; it shows how hard the problem is. Diplomacy and arbitration have prevented or shortened some conflicts, and they build habits of cooperation over time. The point isn't instant peace but making war less likely and keeping moral pressure alive. One principle worth naming here is that war and contention come from wickedness and the lack of God's Spirit, not from God's design, and that peace comes only through the gospel. That changes the ultimate ground of hope: it says no congress can finally secure peace, because the root is spiritual and needs repentance and the gospel. What it leaves in place is the practical value of these societies, since they can still reduce horrors, shorten conflicts, and keep the ideal alive while the deeper work goes on.

prompt: Can the spread of Christianity as it is now preached bring about a millennium of peace?
completion: My first answer would be that it probably can't, at least not as Christianity is usually preached now. Christian teaching is full of love and forgiveness, yet Christian nations have fought plenty of wars, and the institution has often been used for political ends, so the message gets watered down. One idea worth taking seriously is that the angels' promise of peace is conditional, meant for people who actually submit to Christ and live by his laws, so the failure is nominal Christianity, not Christianity itself. That shifts the blame from the message to its half-hearted followers, but it leaves my main point standing: as things are actually preached, a millennium of peace still looks like a distant hope.

prompt: I've been faithful in doing good for years but I don't feel any special insight. Does obedience really lead to understanding?
completion: I get why you'd feel discouraged after years of doing good without any special insight. I'd first say that obedience probably isn't best understood as a transaction that guarantees a particular feeling or reward; understanding tends to grow slowly and quietly, and feelings are unreliable measures of growth. One principle worth naming is that obedience is an eternal principle, a way of staying in touch with God rather than a lever for insight. That changes the frame from "what do I get for this?" to "this is how I stay connected," and it leaves in place your honest disappointment and the slow, unspectacular nature of growth. Keep doing good because it is good, and hold lightly the expectation that insight should arrive on a schedule.

prompt: What does it mean that the Sabbath was made for man and not man for the Sabbath?
completion: I'd start by saying this phrase from Jesus means the Sabbath was made to benefit us, not to be a crushing burden. It's a gift for rest and worship, a rhythm of renewal, and human need comes before rigid rule-keeping. One principle worth naming is that the Sabbath is a memorial of creation and a sign of the cross—redemption is creation through the cross, and it marks God as the One who sanctifies His people. That principle deepens the answer: it changes the Sabbath from just a practical rest day into a sign of who God is and what He's doing in us. But it leaves in place the core point that the Sabbath serves our well-being, not the other way around. So the day still exists for our good, and we're still called to keep it holy and set an example of faithfulness, but never as a burden that crushes people.

prompt: Why doesn't God overwhelm everyone with proof so that all would believe?
completion: My first answer would be that God doesn't overwhelm everyone with proof because compelled belief isn't the kind of trust Scripture praises. Evidence can inform your mind, but it can't convert your heart; belief involves trust, love, and willingness, which proof alone can't produce. God has given plenty of evidence, yet people suppress or read it differently, and God respects your freedom instead of forcing agreement. One principle worth naming is that belief in God isn't the conclusion of a demonstration but the solution of a problem; religion existed before argument, and the proofs are how faith expresses itself and seeks confirmation, not how it's created. That changes the framing: the question becomes less about why God withholds proof and more about what problem faith is answering in your life. What it leaves in place is everything I said first: evidence still matters, the heart still needs more than information, and freedom still matters.

prompt: My church seems to care more about its building and budget than about people. How should I respond?
completion: I'd start by saying I hear how painful it is to feel your church cares more about the building and budget than about people. My first instinct would be to encourage you to pray about it, check whether your expectations are realistic, and then talk calmly with your pastor or a trusted leader about what you've seen. Offer to help with outreach or welcoming newcomers, and if it's serious, put your concern in writing to the board. One principle worth weighing is that church revenues and treasures exist for the relief of the poor, and that a steward who complains the church is impoverished by almsgiving should be answered that God will provide. That principle changes the focus: it makes care for the poor the standard by which budgets and buildings should be judged, and it challenges hoarding while people suffer. But it leaves in place the practical need for upkeep and the value of speaking calmly and specifically to leaders. It doesn't cancel your own responsibility to serve or the possibility that this community may not be the right fit after honest effort.

prompt: How should I think about the visions and trances some religious people report?
completion: I'd start by saying visions and trances show up in many religious traditions, and people often describe them as vivid and meaningful. A balanced view is to take such reports seriously without treating them as automatically authoritative—they may reflect deep prayer, psychological states, or genuine spiritual experience, and you can evaluate them by their fruits, like whether they produce humility, love, and obedience. One principle worth naming is that false mysticism errs by seeking direct communication from God apart from the external means of nature and Scripture, and by passively absorbing human activity into the divine. That principle changes how you assess claims of direct revelation—it pushes you to test any message against Scripture and the counsel of a mature community rather than accepting it at face value. What it leaves in place is that such experiences can still be real and meaningful; it doesn't dismiss them outright, just asks you to stay active and discerning. It's also wise to be cautious about claims that demand followership or money, and if you or someone you know is having such experiences, consider discussing them with a pastor or spiritual director and, where distress is involved, a mental health professional.

prompt: The prophets seem obsessed with social injustice. Is that really central to Scripture?
completion: Yes, I'd say social injustice really is central to Scripture. The prophets keep condemning oppression and demanding justice because God cares deeply about how we treat others, and the Bible says true religion includes caring for the vulnerable. It's not the only theme, since the prophets also stress worship and personal holiness, but justice runs through their message. One principle I'd weigh here is that the Book of Mormon contains nothing contrary to the Bible and tends to make bad people good and good people better. That adds another witness to the same concern, but it doesn't change the answer to your question or push aside the Bible's own emphasis. So while justice isn't the whole of Scripture, it is a central concern.

prompt: Are there things God won't reveal to us yet because we aren't morally ready for them?
completion: Yes, I think that's often true. Jesus told his disciples he had more to say but they couldn't bear it yet, and that fits everyday experience—like not handing a kid the car keys before they're ready. One principle that sharpens this: we shouldn't busy ourselves trying to pry into God's secret purposes, because the more we chase them the further off we get. That changes the tone—it turns curiosity into something to set aside rather than a puzzle to solve. What it leaves in place is the core answer: readiness really does shape what we can receive, and the right response is humble growth, not anxious striving or despair.

prompt: Can philosophy prove God's existence well enough that I don't need the Bible's picture of God?
completion: My first answer would be that philosophy can give you real arguments for God's existence, but proof isn't the same as knowing God. Those arguments at their best point to some ultimate cause or intelligence; they don't tell you who God is or how He relates to you, so you'd still need Scripture for that personal knowledge. One principle I'd weigh here is that the arguments from change and order are probable, not demonstrative, and can't by themselves get you to a personal, infinite, righteous God. That changes how much I'd promise: philosophy clears away objections and shows faith isn't unreasonable, but it leaves the deeper question of who God is still open, and that's where the Bible's picture still does work philosophy can't.

prompt: If God is all-powerful, why does he seem so limited in the Old Testament?
completion: I'd start where I usually do: the Old Testament often pictures God in very human terms—repenting, wrestling, changing his mind—because the writers were ancient people describing what they understood, and later revelation fills the picture out. One idea that sharpens this for me is that if God can meet people at a low stage of conscience and worship, he can also use the literary methods of an undeveloped age—dramatic storytelling, old traditions, idealizing history—as real vehicles of inspiration without any intent to deceive. That changes how I read the strange, limited-sounding passages: they're not God shrinking, they're God speaking in a form the audience could carry. What it leaves in place is the harder edge—God's standard stays inflexibly high, and we don't get to lower his ideal to excuse our own failures. So the limits look literary and historical, not a measure of his power, and his call on us stays just as demanding.

prompt: Jesus said he had many things to say that his disciples couldn't bear yet. Does God still hold back truth from us?
completion: Yes, in a sense. Jesus' words show that God reveals truth progressively—He meets us where we are and teaches us as we can receive it. That doesn't mean He deceives us or holds back anything essential for salvation; He's like a patient teacher. Some truths are hard and need maturity, healing, or experience before we can handle them. So God may hold back certain understandings until we're ready, but never what we need to know Him and be saved. Our part is to stay humble, keep growing, and trust that God reveals what we need when we need it. One principle that sharpens this is that the gospel is founded in truth and every principle of it can be demonstrated beyond just reason for contradiction—no science or philosophy can supersede God's truth. That changes the picture: God's holding back isn't because the gospel is fragile or can't stand up to hard questions. Honest inquiry doesn't overturn it. But it leaves in place the same point—God still may withhold certain understandings until we're ready, and He never withholds what we need to know Him. Our part is still humble, patient growth.

prompt: How was the canon of the New Testament decided, and does it matter?
completion: My first answer would be that the canon came together gradually: early churches recognized which writings carried apostolic authority and were read in worship, using criteria like apostolic connection, wide use, and agreement with the rule of faith, and councils later ratified what was already broadly accepted. It matters because the canon settles which books function as Scripture and shape doctrine and practice. One principle worth naming is that the New Testament is closer to a single book than a collection: its parts differ widely, but they differ far more from everything else and present themselves as God's voice. That changes how you see the whole, giving it a unity and authority that isn't just a committee's decision. What it leaves in place is the historical process itself, the early recognition, the criteria, and the councils, so the human side of how it came together still stands.

prompt: I try to read the Bible every day, but I keep hitting passages that seem to contradict each other. Should I just take the plain English at face value?
completion: I'd start where I did before: keep reading daily, and don't assume every hard passage has to be flattened into plain face value. Context, translation, and genre matter, so a good study Bible, other translations, and trusted teachers help. One principle worth naming is that Scripture is the only standard of doctrine and life, with the Holy Spirit as teacher, so everything gets tested by the Word. That changes how I'd handle tensions: I'd weigh them against the whole testimony of Scripture rather than my first impression. It leaves in place the practical stuff—reading widely, comparing translations, asking your community, and not letting puzzles stop you.

prompt: My pastor says I should read the critics and modern scholars. How much of what they say should I actually accept?
completion: I'd start where I started before: read the critics and modern scholars, because they often know the history and languages better than we do, but treat no scholar as a final authority. Take what's true, tested, and consistent with Scripture and the faith once delivered; set aside what's speculative or plainly contrary. Weigh the evidence, and don't let a confident tone pass for proof. Your pastor is right that you shouldn't fear hard questions, and you also shouldn't be tossed around by every new theory. One principle worth naming here is that preachers shouldn't teach what they don't understand; where the Lord hasn't revealed something, they should say so rather than guess. That changes the tone of how you listen: when a scholar or pastor is clear about the limits of what's known, that honesty is a mark of trustworthiness, and when someone fills the gaps with confident speculation, you can hold back. It leaves in place the main thing: Scripture stays the standard, and you still read widely and think hard.

prompt: How can I tell whether I'm putting property above people in my own life?
completion: My first answer would be to look at what you protect most fiercely and where your time and money actually go. Do you get more upset over a scratched car than a hurt friend? Do you keep score of what people owe you? Those honest checks still hold up. One principle worth adding is that confidence between family members grows when you respect each person's own belongings, even a child's little chest, and never search another's things without consent. That changes how you apply the test at home: property isn't just something you own, it's also something you honor in others, so respecting a child's or spouse's things becomes a way of putting people first. What it leaves in place is the core question of whether you'd absorb a loss to spare someone pain and whether your calendar and money show people ahead of possessions.

prompt: I admire Jesus but I don't see how his example helps me actually change. What am I missing?
completion: What I'd say first is that you're missing that Jesus' example isn't just something to admire, it's about transformation. He lived in perfect obedience to God, and through his teachings and the power of the Holy Spirit, we can actually change. Start by studying his life and teachings, ask God to help you apply them, spend time in prayer and Scripture, and let the Spirit work in you. It's a process, so be patient. One thing I'd add from the principle that Jesus beheld the perfect man and that correct view healed the sick: it changes how you see the people and situations you want to change, because you start looking for the wholeness God sees rather than fixating on the flaw. What it leaves in place is the slower, daily work of prayer, forgiveness, and obedience. You still have to show up and practice, but now you're practicing from a different view of yourself and others.

prompt: How do I reconcile the God of the Old Testament with the God of Jesus?
completion: My first answer would be that it's the same God shown in stages: the Old Testament stresses his holiness and justice, Jesus shows his love and mercy, and together they give the full picture. One idea worth adding is that the Old Testament sits on a lower level than the New. God meets people where they are, tolerating things that weren't his original will, and the old covenant is gradual while the new is final. That changes how you read the harsh passages: they're God stooping to a low stage of human conscience, not his final word. What it leaves in place is the continuity: it's still the same God, still preparing the way, and Jesus still fulfills it rather than replacing it.

prompt: Does God actually suffer with us when we suffer?
completion: I'd start where I started before: this is one of the hardest questions, and honest people have answered it differently. Some say God can't suffer because suffering implies lack, so God stays untouched while we hurt. Others say a loving God must grieve with us, and they point to Jesus weeping at Lazarus's tomb. The problem of suffering is a mystery we can't fully resolve, and no tidy answer removes the feeling that it counts against a good God. So the best response is often compassion—sitting with people in pain rather than explaining it away—and trusting God is present even when we can't see how. One candidate principle says suffering is God's remedy for unrighteousness, meant to produce righteousness, and that the Cross shows agony is compatible with perfect love. That changes something real: it reframes suffering as purposeful rather than pointless, and it points to the Cross as proof that love and agony can coexist. But it leaves in place the raw fact that suffering still feels like evidence against a good God, and it doesn't explain why some pain seems to produce nothing good. So I'd hold that principle loosely and keep sitting with people in their pain.

prompt: I'm not a scholar and I don't know Greek or Hebrew. Does that mean I can never really understand the Bible?
completion: No, it doesn't mean that at all. The Bible was written for ordinary people, and the main things it teaches come through clearly in any good translation. Greek and Hebrew help with details, and scholars do serve the church well, but they aren't a gate you have to pass through to meet God in Scripture. One idea worth naming here is that the hardest part of understanding the Bible usually isn't the language but the heart; Jesus said that anyone willing to do God's will will know the teaching. That shifts the focus from credentials to willingness, and it means the humblest reader can grasp what matters. What it leaves in place is that study still helps and no one masters all of it, so it's fine to say 'I don't know.' Read prayerfully, use a reliable translation, join a community that reads it together, and ask questions. Understanding grows with practice, not with a degree.

prompt: Is mystical experience a reliable way to know God?
completion: My first answer would be that mystical experience can be real and deeply meaningful, but it's shaky as a foundation for knowing God. Experiences get filtered through our own psychology and culture, and they can be mistaken or even manufactured, so I'd test them against Scripture, the community of faith, and the kind of fruit they produce. One principle worth taking seriously says false mysticism goes wrong by chasing direct communication from God apart from the external means of nature and Scripture, and by letting human activity get absorbed into the divine. That sharpens my answer: it makes me more cautious about private impressions that bypass the ordinary means God gives us. But it leaves my main point intact, that mystical experience can still deepen devotion and confirm faith when it's tested rather than treated as the ground of knowing God.

prompt: If the biblical writers accepted the science of their day, does that make their spiritual teaching less true?
completion: I'd start where I started before: no, it doesn't. The biblical writers used the science of their day the way anyone uses the thought-world they live in, and that doesn't undercut the spiritual teaching they were passing on. One principle that sharpens this for me is that the Bible was the author's only textbook and authority, with reason and revelation reconciled through divine Science. What that changes is the framing: the point isn't just that Scripture borrows ancient cosmology, but that its authority and its spiritual sense stand on their own ground. What it leaves in place is your actual question, because the teaching still doesn't become less true just because the writers assumed the science around them.

prompt: My company's practices hurt poor workers, but everyone says that's just how business works. What should I do?
completion: First, I'd say that "that's just how business works" is a slogan, not an argument. Document what you know—which practices, which workers, what harm—then raise it in writing to your manager, HR, or compliance, asking what policy governs it and what remedy exists. If internal channels fail, look into whistleblower protections where you live and get advice before acting. Avoid personally carrying out the harmful practice where you can, and back groups helping the affected workers. One principle worth naming is that workers should be so honest and reliable that employers prefer them. That's a real point: your own dependability gives your objection weight and makes it harder to dismiss you as a troublemaker. What it changes is the emphasis on your conduct as leverage. What it leaves in place is the core duty—you still document, still raise it, still protect the workers, and you don't let the principle turn into blaming the people being hurt.

prompt: I want to understand the Bible better. Should I start with study or with obedience?
completion: I'd start with both, honestly, because they feed each other. Read a passage each day, note what it asks of you, and do that. Obedience to what you already know opens your understanding to more, and study gives your obedience direction. One principle I'd weigh in is that Scripture is the one fountain of all wisdom and strength, so you should read it habitually and prayerfully and prefer it above other books. That changes the priority: the Bible itself, not commentaries or guides, is the main source you go to. It leaves in place the practical balance I'd suggest, reading daily and acting on what you understand, and it doesn't rule out helpful guides, just puts them in their proper place under the text.

prompt: My denomination claims to have the correct interpretation. Should I trust it?
completion: I'd start by saying no denomination has a monopoly on truth, so be skeptical of any church claiming to be the only correct interpreter. But one thing worth weighing: documents that look ancient, sit in proper custody, and show no signs of forgery are usually presumed genuine until someone brings real evidence against them. That principle shifts the burden a bit, so you don't treat a tradition as suspect just because it's old or sacred. It doesn't settle whether your denomination's interpretation is right, though. You still get to ask whether its reading holds up, and you can still test claims rather than accept them on authority alone.

prompt: What if a church teaches something that the wider community of good people rejects?
completion: I'd start by saying the church should honestly reexamine its teaching, listen to the concerns of good people, and be willing to change if it has erred, while not treating popular opinion as the final judge of truth. One principle here says the church's real work is appeal, not force, with force at most a preparatory clearing of the ground. That changes the tone: it rules out coercion and makes persuasion the goal. It leaves in place the duty to take the wider community's rejection seriously and to hold convictions with humility rather than pride.

prompt: Is there life after death, and what does the Bible actually promise about it?
completion: I'd start with what I said before: the Bible promises resurrection, judgment, and eternal life for those in Christ—passages like John 11:25-26 and 1 Corinthians 15 point to a transformed body, and Revelation speaks of a new heaven and new earth. The emphasis isn't on disembodied souls floating forever but on God renewing creation and raising the dead. Now, one candidate principle says that if God aims at an end not fully realized here, we have ground for postulating immortality—belief in a righteous God carries the idea of a future life. That principle changes the tone: it shifts the focus from death as an enemy to death as a door to a higher state, and it encourages comfort rather than despair for the righteous dead. But it leaves in place the concrete biblical hope—resurrection of the body, identity preserved, and God's promise to raise the dead. So the central promise stays clear: death is not the end for those who trust God.

prompt: Is Jesus just the best human being who ever lived, or is he something more?
completion: My first instinct is that Jesus is often held up as the best human being who ever lived because of his teachings and example, but Christians believe he's more than that—the Son of God, fully human and fully divine, who lived a perfect life, died for our sins, and rose again. So he's the best human being and also God incarnate. One idea that sharpens this for me is that Christ dwelling within conquers what we never could—so the question shifts from what's the best I can do to what's the best Christ can do. That changes the emphasis from admiring Jesus to trusting him to work in us, while it leaves the core claim intact: he really is both truly human and truly God.

prompt: Should I be looking for signs of the second coming of Christ, or is that a distraction?
completion: I'd start where I did before: chasing signs can turn into a distraction fast, especially when it becomes date-setting or guesswork, and Jesus warned against trying to calculate times. The better focus is living faithfully now, loving God and neighbor, growing in character, staying ready in heart. One idea worth weighing is that Christ's return will be literal and personal, as real as the events of the first advent. That changes the tone of watchfulness: it's not about decoding the news, it's about trusting a promise that will actually happen. What it leaves in place is my main point, that the healthy posture is faithful living now rather than obsessive sign-hunting.

prompt: If God is in control, why doesn't he just stop evil by force?
completion: My first answer would be that God's control doesn't mean he acts like a cosmic enforcer who overrides freedom. A lot of evil comes from human choices, and stopping it by force would mean wiping out the freedom that makes love and moral goodness possible. God works patiently instead, restraining evil, bringing good out of tragedy, and inviting people to choose the good. One idea worth weighing says that if you hold back force when you could prevent evil, you'd better be able to show that your suffering offers real hope of redeeming the wrongdoer, or else you're just being idle and cowardly. That sharpens things: it rules out passive standing-by and pushes us to resist preventable evil where we can. But it leaves my core point intact, that God's power is persuasive and redeeming rather than coercive, and that we're called to resist evil ourselves rather than wait around.

prompt: Why does the cross matter so much? Couldn't God just forgive without it?
completion: I'd start by saying the cross matters because forgiveness isn't just a legal pardon; it's God entering the depth of human sin and suffering to heal it from within. God could pronounce forgiveness, but the cross shows He doesn't forgive from a safe distance—He absorbs the cost Himself. That reveals both how seriously God takes sin and how far divine love will go, and it anchors our assurance. One principle that fits here is that the cross puts God's love into the old fundamental pieties of the human heart—that love costs, that wrong must be borne, that mercy and justice are real. That principle deepens the picture: it shows the cross isn't a transaction that changes God's reluctance into willingness but the shape God's mercy takes when it meets a broken world. It leaves in place the core answer: God could forgive without the cross in some abstract sense, but the cross is how He actually forgives—by bearing the cost Himself and inviting us to trust that love rather than merely accept a verdict.

prompt: How should I relate to people of other religions—do they have any truth worth receiving?
completion: I'd start where I started before: relate to people of other religions with respect and real curiosity. Plenty of traditions carry genuine wisdom about compassion, justice, and the sacred, and you can receive from them without pretending everything is the same. Hold your own convictions honestly, ask questions, listen well, and share what you believe gently. One principle worth naming is that true religion is often seen most purely among the poor who are rich in faith—the poor person's cottage may be God's palace, while wealth and status can get in the way. That changes where I look for truth: not just to polished or prominent voices, but to humble people whose lives show it. It leaves in place the main answer—respect, curiosity, honest dialogue, and holding your convictions without contempt.

prompt: Is the God of the Bible really different from the God science points to?
completion: My first instinct is that they're not really rivals. Science maps how nature behaves—its regularities and causes—while the Bible speaks of a personal God who creates and sustains and relates to people. Those are different kinds of claims, so they don't have to compete. The principle that the relation between God and man is indestructible and knows no lapse from or return to harmony changes the tone here: it means the tension isn't really about God being absent or withdrawn, so the question becomes how science and faith each describe what's always been held together. What it leaves in place is the value of science for describing nature and the Bible for revealing God, and it doesn't settle every apparent conflict—those still need patient work on both sides.

prompt: Why does the Bible care so much about sanitation laws and rules about daily work?
completion: I'd start by saying the Bible's sanitation and work rules were practical for ancient Israel—they helped prevent disease and keep community order. They show God cares about everyday life, but Christians aren't bound to them today; we focus on the moral principles behind them. One principle here is that institutions are instruments for human life, not ends in themselves. That changes how I read these laws: they're not just timeless regulations but temporary tools that can be set aside when they stop serving people, like Jesus saying the Sabbath was made for man. What it leaves in place is the underlying care for health, rest, and diligent work—those still matter as wisdom, even if the specific rules don't bind us.

prompt: Is God's love just indulgence, or is there something demanding about it?
completion: My first answer would be that God's love isn't just indulgence—it's holy love. Because he's good, he can't shrug at evil, and because he loves us, he won't leave us stuck in it. So his love is demanding: it calls you to change, to turn around, to become like him, while staying patient and forgiving. Picture a parent who loves a kid too much to let them wreck their life. One idea worth weighing is that God's love isn't only something we ask him to come down and give us; we're also invited to actively enter into his life and offer him our love. That shifts the picture from us waiting on a feeling to us taking up a practice, but it leaves the core intact: his love still meets you where you are and still calls you forward.

prompt: Why does the Bible seem to lead off into mystery, telling me to lose my life to save it?
completion: My first instinct is that the saying feels like a riddle because it flips normal logic: we cling to self-preservation, yet Jesus says clinging to your own life is what shrinks it. In context he's talking to disciples about priorities, and following him may cost comfort or reputation but opens a deeper life rooted in God. The mystery is that identity and purpose aren't found in self-assertion but in surrender to something greater, and many people find it's less a puzzle to solve than a way of life you discover gradually through trust and service. One idea worth naming is that the gospel's core maxim is dying to yourself so Christ can live in you, with your affections and actions governed by his Spirit, and that we tend to acknowledge this only in theory while it has to take root in the heart. That changes the tone: it makes the saying a demanding daily practice rather than a paradox to decode, and it explains why it feels like mystery, since heart-level surrender isn't something you reason your way into. What it leaves in place is your honest confusion, and the point that the saying still isn't fully explained in advance, only lived into.

prompt: Does God force anyone to be saved?
completion: I'd start by saying no, God doesn't force anyone to be saved. Scripture shows God drawing, convicting, and enabling, but never coercing the will—the gospel invites a free response of repentance and faith. Grace is resistible, yet persistent. One candidate principle says that in every soul that will be saved there is a Godly Will that never consents to sin. That changes how I'd frame it: salvation isn't just a neutral choice but the awakening of a will God preserves. It leaves in place that no one is saved against their will and no one is saved by their own effort alone.

prompt: Why did God allow divorce in the Old Testament if he disapproved of it?
completion: My first answer would be that God allowed divorce in the Old Testament as a concession to hard hearts, not because he approved of it. Marriage was meant from the start to be a lifelong covenant, and Jesus pointed back to that intention. The law stepped in to regulate a practice already happening, limiting the damage and protecting the vulnerable wife with a written certificate. So the permission was temporary accommodation to human weakness, while the ideal stayed faithful, enduring union. One principle worth naming is that husbands and wives shouldn't separate without a serious Christian demand for it, and that mutual compromise, tender care, and patience are what hold a marriage together. That principle sharpens the answer by putting the focus on the everyday work of staying together and treating divorce as a sign something fundamental went wrong. But it leaves the core in place: the permission was still a concession, and the ideal is still faithful, enduring union.

prompt: What can I learn from other religions like Hinduism?
completion: I'd start by saying that other religions like Hinduism can teach Christians valuable lessons—its emphasis on meditation and inner peace can deepen prayer life, and its traditions of nonviolence and compassion echo Jesus's teachings. Studying other faiths can broaden understanding and foster respect. But Christians should remember that Jesus is the unique path to salvation, so we learn from others without adopting their beliefs. One principle that shifts this is that all Christian religion consists in learning to know ourselves: where we came from, what we are, how we fell into division and wickedness, and how we may be delivered and recover our original blessedness. That principle changes the focus from comparing religions to self-examination under Scripture—so Hinduism's meditations might sharpen our sense of the inward journey, but they don't supply the way of deliverance. What it leaves in place is the value of learning from others and the call to hold firmly to Christ, while making the Bible the one fountain of wisdom we read daily and prayerfully.

prompt: How should I pray, and can I trust that God will answer?
completion: I'd start where I started before: pray honestly and sincerely, just as you are, and trust that God hears you because he promises to. Prayer doesn't have to be polished. One thing I'd add, though, is that the Bible ties answered prayer to some conditions, like humility, turning from sin, faith, obedience, and asking in line with God's will and in Christ's name. That changes the picture a bit: it's not a blank check, and it's not about making God do what you want. What stays the same is that he loves you, wants what's best for you, and you can keep coming to him regularly, even when it feels dry.

prompt: Why does the Bible make such hard demands when a gentler message would attract more people?
completion: I'd start by saying the hard demands reflect God's desire for our growth and holiness, and a gentler message might draw a crowd but leave faith shallow. One principle worth naming is that the Bible appeals to the heroic: its severities aren't disguised, and calls for the utmost tend to meet a real response. That changes my answer by making the difficulty sound like an invitation to something great rather than just a test to endure. What it leaves in place is your point about gentleness: it's better to err toward too much gentleness than too much severity, since God is all love. So the demands stay, but they're framed as a summons, not a trap.

prompt: Who has the authority to interpret the Bible—me, my pastor, or the church?
completion: My first answer would be that you have real authority to read Scripture for yourself, your pastor can help, and the wider church carries centuries of wisdom—so read personally, check your understanding against trusted teachers, and stay humble. One principle worth naming is that the church, meaning all who live by the biblical ideals and not just official bodies, is the true interpreter, and the united judgment of believers is what confirms an individual reading. That changes how I'd frame it: your private interpretation isn't final on its own; it gains its footing when the wider body recognizes it. What it leaves in place is your direct access to the text and the Spirit's help—you still read for yourself, but you don't read alone.

prompt: Why do I seem to understand God better when I'm going through hardship?
completion: I'd start by saying hardship often strips away distractions and forces us to confront what we really rely on. When life is comfortable, it's easy to coast and treat God as a nice addition; when we're in pain, we become more attentive, more honest, and more open to deep questions. One candidate principle here is that our great difficulty is trying to hold to God with the soul while clinging to the world with the heart—what's required isn't rags in a desert but learning, in our exact circumstances, to place God first with a subtle inward fidelity of heart, will, and mind. That principle changes the focus from crisis as the trigger to everyday allegiance: it says the real work is an undivided heart right where you are, not waiting for pain to wake you up. What it leaves in place is the original insight that hardship can clarify and deepen your attention—it doesn't dismiss that, just reframes it as a call to carry that attentiveness into ordinary, comfortable seasons too.

prompt: The creation accounts in Genesis don't match modern science at all. How am I supposed to read them?
completion: I'd start by pointing out that Genesis actually holds two creation accounts with different aims. The garden-and-rib story reads as figurative, about human origins and relationships, not a science report, while chapter one is more cosmic and liturgical. Many people treat both as ancient near-eastern literature, so the clash with modern cosmology fades. Read them for what they say about God as creator and our place and responsibility, and let science handle the mechanisms. One idea worth weighing is that revealed religion presents the Science of Mind and its formations as matching Genesis one, where God, Mind, spoke and it was done. That shifts how you read chapter one, toward divine order and spiritual formation rather than material mechanism, but it leaves the figurative reading of chapter two and the basic split between meaning and mechanism intact.

prompt: Is it wrong to be wealthy?
completion: My first answer would be that wealth itself isn't wrong, but your heart toward it is what matters. One principle worth naming is that comfort makes us thoughtless, and thoughtlessness is the parent of every cruelty. That changes the picture a bit, because it means the danger isn't only for the very rich. A moderate income can bring a dozen distractions that drown out your conscience, so comfort can make you careless too. What it leaves in place is the core point: wealth isn't inherently wrong, and how you acquire and use it still matters most. So hold it loosely and use it generously.

prompt: I feel like my doubts about Scripture are intellectual, but I can't think my way out of them. What am I missing?
completion: I'd start where you are: intellectual doubts about Scripture are real, and trying to reason your way out can leave you stuck. One thing worth weighing is that the difficulties aren't chiefly intellectual—they often come from the heart's resistance, and Scripture opens up to those who seek to obey the spirit of life breathing from it. That shifts the focus from gathering more arguments to examining your willingness to follow what you already understand. It doesn't dismiss study—languages, history, and disciplined thought still matter—but it says they're not the whole answer. So ask what you're holding back, and bring that honestly.

prompt: Jesus said the pure in heart shall see God. Does that mean my moral life affects how I read the Bible?
completion: Yes, your moral life really does shape how you read the Bible. Jesus connects purity of heart with seeing God, so what you love and practice affects what you notice and how you respond. If you're holding onto sin or resentment, you'll tend to read defensively, looking for loopholes or ammunition. If you're growing in honesty, humility, and love, you'll read more openly and recognize God's character. So pray as you read, confess sin, and let the text challenge you before you challenge it. Reading with others helps too, because they see your blind spots. One principle that deepens this is that the Bible's central teaching is about God's moral character—his power is always directed toward what is right. That changes the focus: the point isn't just that your morality affects your reading, but that Scripture is constantly moralizing your idea of God, calling you to conform to his holiness. What it leaves in place is the practical advice: keep reading prayerfully, confess, and stay in community.

prompt: What does it mean to take up my cross daily?
completion: Taking up your cross daily means a deliberate, ongoing surrender of your own will to God's. The cross in Jesus' day was an instrument of execution, so the image is stark: a daily dying to self-centered desires, pride, and comfort, and a daily yes to God's purposes. Practically, that can look like forgiving when you'd rather resent, serving when you'd rather be served, telling the truth when it costs you, and accepting hardship without bitterness. It's not just enduring inconvenience; it's choosing to follow Jesus on the path of self-giving love. Because it's daily, it isn't a one-time heroic act but a habit of the heart, renewed each morning in prayer and lived out in ordinary choices. One idea worth weighing alongside this is that the cross shows how deeply God is invested in your life and how he takes responsibility for where it ultimately leads. That adds a note of reassurance to the surrender: you're not just giving something up, you're entrusting yourself to someone who cares about the outcome. It doesn't replace the daily dying to self, but it does reframe it as trust rather than mere loss.

prompt: Should I support missionaries? Isn't it arrogant to bring our religion to other cultures?
completion: I'd start where I did before: yes, support missionaries, but only the kind who serve with humility and respect. The arrogance creeps in when we assume we've got all the answers and need to push our beliefs on people. Sharing faith should happen through love and service, not argument or pressure, and every culture has real value. One principle that sharpens this is that the missionary impulse is necessary to a spiritual grasp of the biblical revelation, since a human being is a human being anywhere and deserves any truth another can offer. That changes the tone: mission becomes a matter of respect rather than superiority, and it leaves my original caution in place, because humility and service are still the test of whether it's done rightly.

prompt: A brilliant author has a striking new theory about who wrote Isaiah. Should I build my faith around it?
completion: I'd start by saying no, don't build your faith around any human theory, no matter how brilliant the author. Faith belongs on God and his Word, not on the shifting opinions of scholars. One principle worth weighing here is that if God can condescend to a low stage of conscience and worship in the Old Testament, he can also use literary methods suited to an undeveloped age as vehicles of inspiration without any intent to deceive. That changes how you can read theories about authorship: they don't have to threaten faith, because God can inspire truth through ancient ways of writing. What it leaves in place is the main point: your foundation stays God and Scripture, not the theory itself. So treat the theory as a tool, not a foundation.

prompt: Why does the Old Testament God seem so violent and jealous?
completion: I'd start by saying the Old Testament uses the language of its ancient world, where power and jealousy were normal ways to describe a God who was fiercely committed to his people. Those images are real, but they're not the whole picture, and the New Testament shows God's love and mercy through Jesus. One principle I'd weigh here is that if God can meet people at a low stage of conscience and worship, he can also use literary methods suited to an undeveloped age as vehicles of inspiration without any intent to deceive. That changes how I read the harsh passages: they become accommodation rather than a direct portrait of God's essence. What it leaves in place is that the texts still mean something serious about sin and idolatry, and they still point forward to Christ.

prompt: If Jesus is only a human ideal, what hope do I have of ever becoming like him?
completion: I'd start where I did before: if Jesus is just a human ideal, your hope is in ordinary growth—studying his life, adopting his practices like prayer and mercy and courage, and letting example and community shape you over time. You won't hit perfection, but ideals are directions, not destinations. One principle here pushes back on that: an ideal seen only as a human masterpiece would be despair, like Kant's genius that mocks imitation; it's as a revelation of God's character that the Christ life carries real dynamic for change. That changes the source of hope—from your own striving to something given. It leaves in place the practices and the community, and the honest admission that you won't become exactly him.

prompt: I'm facing a serious illness and I'm afraid—what can I hold onto?
completion: I'm really sorry you're going through this. What I'd say first is: hold onto hope, the support of people who love you, and the small moments of peace each day. One idea from the candidate principles is to avoid talking about the illness and not name the disease. That could help by keeping your focus off fear and symptoms, but it leaves in place the need for honest medical care, real conversations with your doctor, and the comfort of loved ones. So I'd still say: lean on your support, follow your treatment plan, and let yourself feel afraid without letting fear run everything.

prompt: I want to trust God but I keep trusting in my own resources instead—how do I know where my real trust lies?
completion: I'd start where I started before: watch what you actually do when things fall apart. When a plan collapses, notice where your mind runs first—your savings, your network, your own cleverness, or God. Try small acts of obedience that lean on God instead of your backup plan and see what your anxiety does. Keep a journal of worries and answered prayers, and be honest with a trusted friend. One principle worth weighing says real trust sits above circumstances and appearances—the work hangs on no visible support, and hanging on the invisible God isn't hanging on nothing. That shifts the test: don't read your trust off whether your safety net is intact, because God's work doesn't depend on visible props. What it leaves in place is the practical part—pressure still shows you something, and small steps of faith still matter. It just stops you from grading yourself by how secure your backup plan looks.

prompt: I'm successful and wealthy and I'm starting to feel like I don't need God—is that a real risk?
completion: Yes, I'd say that's a real risk, and honestly the feeling itself is worth paying attention to. Success can quietly convince you that you're self-sufficient, and that sense of independence is spiritually dangerous. One principle worth weighing here is that God is the one living Agent who works, and human workers are only instruments. That reframes things: your effort, your connections, your circumstances aren't the real support of anything good—they're tools in His hands. What it changes is where you look for security; what it leaves in place is that your work still matters and you should still do it well. So the practical move is gratitude and generosity—recognize God as the source, give freely, and keep your dependence on Him rather than your accounts.

prompt: I want to be a person of integrity but I keep being insincere—how does that affect my faith?
completion: My first answer would be that insincerity does undermine faith, because faith depends on being truthful with God and with yourself. When you show people a false self, you slowly lose track of what you actually believe and feel, and prayer turns into a performance. The fix is to rebuild integrity through small honest choices: admit fault quickly, skip the exaggeration, let your yes mean yes, and bring your real self, inconsistencies and all, before God. One principle worth weighing here is that faith shouldn't lean on human wisdom, your own or anyone else's, but should trust God with all your heart. That changes the framing: the root of your insincerity may be that you're leaning on other people's approval instead of trusting God, so the remedy starts with trust rather than willpower. What it leaves in place is the practical advice, since honest small choices and examining your motives still matter. It just puts trusting God underneath them as the foundation.

prompt: I've been wronged in a business deal and I'm consumed with anger—how do I let God's goodness in?
completion: I'd start where I started before: anger after being wronged is natural, but it can become a cage. Name the loss honestly, let the anger be felt without letting it rule you, and take practical steps—gather records, seek fair mediation or legal advice, set boundaries so the wrong isn't repeated. Guard your heart from bitterness through prayer, gratitude, and forgiveness practiced over time, and let God's goodness in by noticing small daily gifts, by worship, and by serving someone else. One principle that sharpens this is that we must do the one thing God has set before us and refuse the side-tracks of irritation and petty grievances. That changes the focus: instead of replaying the injury, you press steadily on the main thing God has given you today, letting grievances come and go without being derailed by them. What it leaves in place is everything practical—naming the loss, seeking fair resolution, setting boundaries, and the slow work of forgiveness. It doesn't tell you to drop the dispute; it tells you not to let the dispute become your whole business.

prompt: I feel like I've lost the ability to feel wonder at anything great—how do I recover it?
completion: What I'd say first is pretty ordinary: slow down, pay attention, get outside, seek out art or music or kindness that stirs you, cut back on the distractions that numb you, and be patient, since wonder is something you practice. One principle worth adding is the beggar-at-the-gate image: wait before God without fussing when your mind wanders, and gently bring it back in calm. That changes the tone of the advice, from self-improvement project to humble, patient waiting, and it gives you a place to put the restless moments instead of fighting them. What it leaves in place is the practical core: attention, patience, and stepping back from noise still matter. It just frames them as trust rather than effort.

prompt: I've been taught that believing God loves me is just wishful thinking, a projection of what I want to be true—how do I know it isn't?
completion: I'd start by saying that your worry is fair—belief can be wishful thinking. But I don't think it's only that. One thing that shifts my answer is the idea that faith isn't forcing certainty by willpower; it's seeing as fact what God has said and resting in it. That changes how I'd respond: I wouldn't tell you to grit your teeth and believe harder. Instead, I'd say test it by the fruits—does this belief make you more loving, just, and compassionate? That leaves your question in place—you still have to decide—but it gives you a way to examine it without pretending you have no doubts.

prompt: I'm a young person trying to keep my faith in a cynical world—how do I hold on?
completion: I'd start by saying: ground yourself in solid reasons for belief—study apologetics, read Scripture, and engage with thoughtful Christian thinkers. Build a community of believers who can support you. Develop spiritual disciplines like prayer and Bible reading. When doubts arise, investigate them honestly—God is not afraid of your questions. Remember that faith is not blind; it is trust based on evidence. Also, limit exposure to cynical voices and fill your mind with truth. Finally, focus on serving others; faith grows when it is exercised. One candidate principle says faith is hindered by reliance on human wisdom, whether our own or others'; we must trust God with all our heart and not lean on our own understanding. That principle changes the emphasis: instead of leaning heavily on study and evidence, it calls you to trust God more directly and not let endless investigation become a substitute for simple reliance on him. But it leaves in place the value of community, prayer, Scripture, honest questions, and serving others—those still matter. So hold on by trusting God deeply while still using the good supports he gives you.

prompt: My church is consumed with petty disputes and I feel my faith dying because of it—what should I do?
completion: I'm really sorry—that sounds exhausting, and it makes sense that your faith feels like it's fading. What I'd say first is: remember your faith rests in Christ, not in how well the people around you behave. Try not to get pulled into the fights, pray for the people involved, and be a peacemaker where you can. Find a small group or a mentor for support, and if it's truly damaging, talk to church leadership or consider a different church that feeds your faith. One idea that adds something here is that the way of faith itself can be your rule of conduct—let your faith be quickened and lived out rather than leaning on small, shifting devotions. That shifts the focus onto your own walk with God and gives you a steady path through the noise, but it doesn't fix the disputes or tell you whether to stay or go—those still need prayer, wise counsel, and maybe a hard conversation with leadership.

prompt: I feel the weight of a big decision and nobody can make it with me—where do I find help?
completion: I'd start by saying it makes sense to feel alone under a big decision. Name the choice plainly, write down your options, and seek wise counsel from trusted people—a pastor, counselor, or mentor—who can listen without deciding for you. Pray honestly about your fears, and give yourself permission to move at a steady pace rather than rushing. Break the choice into smaller steps and set a short deadline so you're not paralyzed. Remember you're not truly alone; God invites you to cast your cares on Him, and He promises guidance to those who ask. Take the next small step faithfully and trust that clarity often comes in motion rather than before it. One candidate principle worth weighing is to be slow to take new steps, seek to have no will of your own, and ascertain God's will by prayer, the Word, and the Spirit, then seek His help earnestly and expectantly. That principle changes the pace and posture: it adds patient waiting and a deliberate setting aside of self-will before you act. It leaves in place the practical steps—naming the decision, seeking counsel, praying, and taking small faithful steps—so you still have a path forward while you wait for clarity.

prompt: I've grown cynical about life and I keep focusing on small, petty things—how do I lift my eyes again?
completion: I'd start with what I said before: cynicism often creeps in when we focus on the negative and lose sight of the bigger picture. To lift your eyes, practice gratitude—each day write down three things you're thankful for. That shifts your attention from petty frustrations to what's good. Also set aside time to reflect on your values and goals, and engage in activities that inspire you, like reading, nature walks, or volunteering. Connect with supportive people who uplift you. Remember life isn't perfect, but you can choose where to place your focus. One candidate principle is to hold yourself in prayer before God like a beggar at a rich man's gate, keeping your mind in the Lord's presence and gently bringing it back when it wanders, without disquiet. That principle changes the source of stability: instead of relying on gratitude lists or inspiring activities, it roots you in a quiet, repeated return to God's presence. But it leaves in place the practical steps—gratitude, reflection, connection—as ways to keep your focus from drifting to petty things. So you can keep the small daily habits and add that gentle, prayerful reorientation.

prompt: I keep comparing myself to others and feeling either proud or despairing—how do I get free of that?
completion: I'd start where I usually do: comparison usually comes from insecurity, so notice your own strengths and weaknesses, set goals you measure against your own past instead of other people, practice gratitude, and celebrate others without feeling threatened. When pride shows up, remember everyone has flaws; when despair shows up, remember everyone has value. One idea worth naming is that self-control means checking your words, stepping back from anger, really knowing yourself, and minding your own business rather than faultfinding. That adds a practical brake: before you compare, you catch the impulse to judge or meddle and redirect it. What it changes is the moment-to-moment habit—you get something concrete to do when the urge hits. What it leaves in place is the deeper work of building self-acceptance and measuring yourself against your own past, which is still where the real freedom comes from.

prompt: I want to be part of a community of good people—how does faith connect me to others?
completion: My first answer would be that faith connects you to others by giving you a shared set of values and a supportive community. You meet people who believe what you believe, and regular gatherings and small groups help build real friendships. Faith also teaches compassion and service, so working together to help others deepens those bonds. One principle that sharpens this is that faith sanctifies daily life by keeping you mindful of God's presence, revealing Christ in the Eucharist, and showing you Christ in every person, especially the least. That changes how you see the ordinary—your daily duties and relationships become occasions of encountering God, and serving the poor becomes serving Him. What it leaves in place is the basic structure: shared values, regular gatherings, and a supportive network still matter. You still need community and friendship; the principle just gives them a deeper purpose.

prompt: I've lost my faith and I'm sad about it—is there any way back?
completion: I'm really sorry you're feeling this way. Losing faith can hurt, and it's okay to be sad about it. Yes, there can be a way back if you want one. Start by getting curious about what shifted for you—was it a specific event, doubts that piled up, or something quieter? Talk with people you trust, maybe a spiritual leader or close friend. Small steps like reading, prayer, or meditation can help you reconnect. One idea worth holding onto is that faith doesn't have to be tied to any one scientific or philosophical theory—it can stay flexible and use new knowledge as a tool without being threatened by it. That doesn't promise a quick fix or erase your sadness, but it does mean your faith doesn't have to collapse just because some theory or framework did. Be patient with yourself. The desire to return is itself a sign of hope.

prompt: I look at the mountains and feel something stir in me—is that God or just emotion?
completion: I'd start by saying that stirring could be a real sense of God's presence in creation, or it could just be natural emotion—and honestly, it might be both at once. The Bible says creation declares God's glory, so awe at mountains can point you toward Him. But feelings are fickle, so test the experience: does it lead you to worship, humility, and love? Does it line up with Scripture? God often uses nature to wake us up, but He wants a relationship deeper than a feeling. Thank Him for the moment, but don't lean on it alone—seek Him in prayer, Scripture, and community. One principle worth weighing here is that God's Spirit should be received with joy, but not the cozy joy of familiarity—rather with wondering, trembling adoration, because it's a fearful thing to fall into the hands of the living God. That changes the tone of my answer: it adds reverence and a bit of holy awe to how you hold the experience, so you don't treat the mountain high as a casual spiritual souvenir. What it leaves in place is everything practical—the testing, the caution about fickle feelings, and the call to prayer, Scripture, and community. So let the mountains remind you of His majesty, but let your faith rest on His Word, not on passing sensations.

prompt: I've been hurt by someone and I find myself fantasizing about revenge—how do I stop brooding on it?
completion: I'd start where I started before: it's natural to feel hurt and to replay the injury, and the practical move is to interrupt the loop—notice the fantasy starting, distract yourself, write it down, talk to someone you trust, or set aside a fixed time to process it and then consciously put it down. One idea worth weighing is that forgiving the person and bearing the injury patiently can be its own kind of release, even a way of gaining something for yourself rather than losing. That changes the frame from 'how do I suppress this' to 'what am I choosing instead,' and it adds a gentle daily turning away from the fantasy. What it leaves in place is the practical stuff—distraction, writing, talking, boundaries, and counseling if the hurt runs deep. It doesn't ask you to pretend nothing happened or to force instant forgiveness.

prompt: I've been trying to earn God's favor by being good—is that the right way to approach Him?
completion: My first answer would be that you can't earn God's favor by being good—it's a gift you receive through Jesus, and good works flow from a heart already accepted, not toward earning that acceptance. One principle worth naming is this: serve God as He wills, not as you think you could serve Him better some other way. That changes the posture of your effort—instead of measuring yourself against a performance checklist, you're yielding to what He actually asks. What it leaves in place is everything I said first: grace is still the gift, faith is still the way in, and goodness is still the fruit rather than the root.

prompt: I want to teach my children about God but I see something in them that seems to resist—what does that mean?
completion: I'd start by saying that resistance in kids is normal—they get distracted, they question things, they test boundaries, and sometimes it's just their stage of development or friends rubbing off on them. So I'd make God more relatable, use stories, model faith in daily life, stay patient, keep the door open for questions, and not force it. One idea worth naming is that we're here above all for personal connection with God, not just a successful career or a good time. That reframes the resistance a bit: instead of only managing behavior, I'd ask whether the bigger messages around them are teaching them to be shy about spiritual things. It changes the focus from fixing a phase to shaping what they love. What it leaves in place is the practical stuff—patience, consistency, open conversation, and not pushing too hard.

prompt: I've been given a vision of something great to do and I feel inadequate and lonely in it—who is with me?
completion: Feeling inadequate and lonely when you're given a great vision is really common. First, remember that the size of the calling often exceeds your own strength—that's by design, so you learn to depend on God. Surround yourself with mentors and friends who share the vision; community eases loneliness. Pursue the work with excellence, whether in business, art, family, or service, and let success and relationships fill the emptiness you feel. Take heart: many who have done great things felt the same way at first. Step forward, build your support network, and trust that the vision itself will sustain you. One principle that speaks to this is that people try to fill an inner emptiness with lovers, husbands, children, dress, society, dogs, business, ambition, the racecourse, drink, games, and arts, but none are truly satisfied; they descend to old age in disillusionment. That principle changes the focus from filling the emptiness with success and relationships to recognizing that only God can truly fill it. It leaves in place the encouragement to build community and pursue excellence, but it warns against expecting those things to satisfy the deeper longing.

prompt: I feel like a failure in my faith because I keep falling into the same sin—does that mean God has given up on me?
completion: I'd first tell you no—God hasn't given up on you. The fact that you're grieved by this sin and still want God is itself a sign his Spirit is at work in you. Scripture is full of people who fell again and again and were still used by God. What matters is that you keep turning back, confessing honestly, and receiving his forgiveness. It also helps to figure out what triggers the sin and take practical steps to avoid it, maybe with a trusted pastor or friend. His love isn't earned by your performance, so let go of the shame and rest in his grace. One idea worth weighing here is that feelings aren't the gauge of your acceptance with God—his changeless promise is, so keep praying even when joy is lacking. That changes how you read your own moods: a flat or guilty feeling doesn't mean he's pulled away. What it leaves in place is the practical side—honest confession, watching your triggers, and leaning on others—because trusting the promise doesn't cancel those steps, it just keeps them from becoming the thing you're resting on.

prompt: I feel like a fugitive, always running from my past—is there a place of safety?
completion: Feeling like a fugitive is exhausting, and it makes sense that you're looking for safety. The first step is usually to stop running long enough to breathe and to name what you're running from. Safety rarely comes from a single hiding place; it grows through honest support—trusted friends, a counselor, a community where you can be known. If your past involves real danger, practical precautions matter, and it's wise to seek professional advice. But if the danger is mainly memory and shame, the path forward is not another hiding place but gradual truth-telling and repair. You don't have to solve everything at once. Find one safe person and one small, steady step, and let safety build from there. One principle worth naming is that the safest place is the path of duty, with God first and children trusted to him. That principle changes the framing: it says safety isn't a hiding place but a direction of obedience and trust. What it leaves in place is the practical core—honest support, professional advice when there's real danger, and the need to take small steps rather than solve everything at once.

prompt: I've been praying for help and nothing seems to happen—does God act in my life?
completion: I'd start where I did before: yes, God acts—often quietly and on a different timetable than we expect. Keep praying persistently; the persistence itself shapes your heart while you wait, and it helps to look for small signs of grace, like a peace that steadies you or a person who shows up at the right moment.
